articles.title: India clinch Champions Trophy with four-wicket win over New Zealand
articles.excerpt: Rohit Sharma's men etched their names into history with a clinical chase to claim their third Champions Trophy title in Dubai.
articles.content:
# India clinch Champions Trophy

India were crowned champions of the ICC Champions Trophy 2025 after a composed four-wicket win over New Zealand in the final at the Dubai International Stadium.

Captain **Rohit Sharma** led from the front with a brisk 19, but it was the experienced middle order that steadied the chase after early jolts. **Virat Kohli** anchored with 48 off 60, while **Hardik Pandya** provided the impetus with a scintillating 45 off 32 deliveries, laced with three fours and two sixes.

## New Zealand post 251

Earlier, asked to bat first, New Zealand recovered from a top-order wobble thanks to **Daryl Mitchell's** 63 and **Tom Latham's** 42. **Glenn Phillips** provided the late flourish with an unbeaten 34 off 30 balls, taking the Black Caps to a competitive 251 for 7.

**Mohammed Shami** was the pick of the bowlers, finishing with 3 for 48, while **Varun Chakravarthy** stifled the middle overs with 1 for 36 in his eight.

## The chase

India lost both openers inside the powerplay, but Kohli and Shreyas Iyer rebuilt with a watchful stand. The asking rate crept over seven, before Pandya walked in and swung the momentum decisively.

## What they said

> "This means the world to us. To win an ICC event after such a long time is special," Rohit said at the presentation.

Captain **Kane Williamson** praised New Zealand's fight: "Credit to India, they were the better side on the day, but I'm proud of how we competed throughout the tournament."

## Key numbers

- India's third Champions Trophy title (2002 shared, 2013, 2025)
- Virat Kohli: 48 runs, his 18th fifty in ICC events
- Mohammed Shami: 9 wickets in the tournament at 16.88

The triumph caps a remarkable turnaround for an Indian side that had not won an ICC ODI event since 2013.
articles.imageCaption: India celebrate with the Champions Trophy after their four-wicket win over New Zealand in the final at the Dubai International Stadium. Photo: Getty Images
articles.author: USA Cricketers staff

articles.title: Border-Gavaskar Trophy: Five things we learned
articles.excerpt: Australia reclaimed the Border-Gavaskar Trophy after a thrilling five-Test series. Here are the key takeaways.
articles.content:
# Five things we learned from the BGT

Australia reclaimed the Border-Gavaskar Trophy for the first time in a decade with a 3-1 series win over India.

## 1. The new Australia

Under **Pat Cummins**, Australia have built a formidable red-ball unit. **Travis Head's** series-defining 140 at Adelaide was the catalyst.

## 2. India's transitional pains

With an ageing top order and a fledgling middle order, India showed flashes but lacked the consistency of past campaigns.

## 3. Bumrah stood alone

**Jasprit Bumrah** was the standout, taking 22 wickets at 14.0 in three Tests. Without him, the series would have been a rout.

## 4. The next generation

**Yashasvi Jaiswal** and **Nitish Reddy** announced themselves on the biggest stage, suggesting India's future is in safe hands.

## 5. The Border-Gavaskar's place

For sheer theatre, there is nothing in Test cricket quite like an Australia-India series contested over five Tests.

articles.author: Daniel Brettig

articles.title: Root, Kohli and Williamson: A statistical comparison
articles.excerpt: How do the Fab Four stack up against each other across formats? We crunch the numbers.
articles.content:
# The Fab Four: By the numbers

**Joe Root**, **Virat Kohli**, **Kane Williamson** and **Steve Smith** have defined an era of batting. Here is how they compare.

## Test runs

- **Joe Root**: 18,452 at 51.5
- **Virat Kohli**: 9,230 at 49.3
- **Steve Smith**: 9,685 at 56.9
- **Kane Williamson**: 8,745 at 49.2

## White-ball mastery

Kohli's ODI numbers - 13,994 runs at 58.7 with 51 centuries - stand apart as the defining white-ball resume of his generation.

## Verdict

Each great offers something distinct. Root's hunger for runs, Smith's unorthodoxy, Williamson's calm, and Kohli's relentlessness - all four are masters of their craft.
articles.author: S Rajesh

articles.title: In conversation with Pat Cummins: leading Australia's golden era
articles.excerpt: The Australia captain on leadership, the World Cup highs, and what drives the most feared pace attack in world cricket.
articles.content:
# In conversation with Pat Cummins

We sat down with **Pat Cummins** to talk about captaining Australia, his fast-bowling craft, and the mentality behind a golden era.

## On captaincy

> "I think the biggest thing I've learned is that you don't have to be the loudest voice in the room. Sometimes the best leadership is just setting the standard with the ball in your hand."

Cummins took over the one-day captaincy at a time of transition and has since lifted both the ODI World Cup and the World Test Championship mace.

## On the World Cup final

> "Ahmedabad was the pinnacle. To chase 240 on that wicket, with the whole of India willing us to lose — that's the kind of day you play cricket for."

## On his bowling

He remains the benchmark for accuracy and pace. His economy rate in white-ball cricket is among the best in the game's history.

> "The yorker is my reset button. When the batter is on top, I go back to what I know I can land nine times out of ten."

## What's next

With a home summer and an away tour of England looming, Cummins is focused on keeping the group hungry.

> "The danger isn't losing — it's thinking you've made it."

articles.title: Bumrah's brilliance: Anatomy of a fast-bowling masterclass
articles.excerpt: A deep dive into what makes Jasprit Bumrah the most lethal fast bowler in world cricket across all formats.
articles.content:
# The Bumrah masterclass

Few fast bowlers in the modern era have commanded the awe that **Jasprit Bumrah** does. His action is unorthodox, his run-up short, yet the carnage he wreaks is remorseless.

## The action

Bumrah's trademark stiff-arm delivery stride generates an extraordinary whip through the crease. His hyperextension at release - the knee bending inward - has been studied by biomechanists for years.

## The yorker

In white-ball cricket, Bumrah's yorker is the gold standard. He lands it on a sixpence under pressure, more often than not swinging it late into the right-hander's base.

> "He is the best in the world at the moment, across formats," said **Pat Cummins** earlier this year.

## Numbers that matter

| Format | Matches | Wickets | Average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test | 36 | 159 | 20.0 |
| ODI | 89 | 149 | 23.0 |
| T20I | 78 | 89 | 17.3 |

The India spearhead remains the benchmark by which fast bowling in this era is measured.

articles.title: Babar Azam: 'I want to be remembered as Pakistan's greatest batter'
articles.excerpt: Pakistan's batting talisman on chasing greatness, handling expectation, and the weight of a nation's hopes.
articles.content:
# Babar Azam: chasing greatness

**Babar Azam** is the batting heartbeat of Pakistan. We spoke to him about his craft, the pressure of carrying a nation, and his ambitions.

## On his technique

> "People talk about elegance, but for me it's about efficiency. Every movement has a purpose. I don't want to waste energy at the crease."

## On the pressure

> "When you walk out in Karachi or Lahore, you're not just playing for yourself. Every person in the stadium has an opinion on your shot selection. You learn to block it out."

## On his goals

Babar's ODI average hovers above 47, with 31 international hundreds. He is blunt about where he wants to end up.

> "I want to be remembered as Pakistan's greatest batter. Not for the averages or the hundreds — for the matches I won."

## On the next generation

> "The young boys coming through — they're fearless. My job is to give them a platform at the top of the order so they can express themselves."

articles.title: Kane Williamson: the calmest man in cricket
articles.excerpt: New Zealand's former captain on serenity at the crease, the World Cup heartbreak, and why temperament trumps talent.
articles.content:
# The calmest man in cricket

**Kane Williamson** has built a career on composure. We spoke about the mindset behind the man.

## On staying calm

> "I think it comes from acceptance. You're going to get out. You're going to have bad days. The trick is not to let one ball cost you two."

## The 2019 World Cup final

> "That day in London — I don't think any of us will ever fully process it. The rules were the rules. We walked off as runners-up, and I was proud of how we carried ourselves."

## On temperament vs talent

> "Talent gets you to the team. Temperament keeps you there. The best batters I've played with aren't always the most gifted — they're the ones who find a way."

## What's next for New Zealand

> "The next generation is ready. My role now is to help them believe they belong at this level."

articles.title: Jasprit Bumrah on the art of the yorker and handling pressure
articles.excerpt: India's pace spearhead on the delivery that defines him, the mindset for the death overs, and learning to trust his body again.
articles.content:
# Bumrah on the yorker

**Jasprit Bumrah** is the most feared fast bowler in the world. We caught up with him to dissect his craft.

## The yorker

> "It's the one ball a batter can't score off if you land it. Everyone talks about pace and bounce, but the yorker is the great equaliser."

## Handling the death overs

> "In the last over, I don't think about the batter. I think about the ball I want to bowl and where my field is. The rest is execution."

## The injury comeback

A stress fracture kept him out for much of 2022. He is candid about the mental toll.

> "When you can't bowl, you question everything. But it taught me patience — to respect my body, to come back smarter, not just harder."

## On captaincy and leadership

> "I don't need the armband to lead. When a young quick comes to me for advice, that's leadership."

articles.title: Shaheen Afridi: Can he rediscover his lethal best?
articles.excerpt: After injuries and a dip in form, Pakistan's spearhead is fighting to get back to the bowler who terrified batters worldwide.
articles.content:
# Shaheen Afridi's search for his best

**Shaheen Afridi** burst onto the scene as a once-in-a-generation left-arm quick. Injuries, however, have tested him.

## The 2021-22 peak

A six-wicket haul at the T20 World Cup against India announced Shaheen to the world. His new-ball spell to **Rohit Sharma** and **KL Rahul** became iconic.

## The injury

A knee injury ruled him out for much of 2022, and he has never quite looked the same force since.

## The road back

Pakistan will need their spearhead at his lethal best for the 2025-26 World Test Championship cycle.
articles.author: Mohammad Isam

articles.title: Shakib Al Hasan: A Bangladesh legend's complicated legacy
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh's greatest cricketer remains as enigmatic as he is brilliant, even as his international career nears its end.
articles.content:
# Shakib's complicated legacy

**Shakib Al Hasan** is, statistically, Bangladesh's greatest cricketer - and one of the finest all-rounders the game has seen.

## The numbers

Nearly 15,000 international runs and almost 700 wickets. Few active players can match the all-round heft of the southpaw from Magura.

## The controversies

And yet, Shakib's career has been punctuated by suspensions, run-ins with the establishment, and a spell away from the game.

## The verdict

When the dust settles, the all-rounder will be remembered as the player who, for two decades, carried Bangladesh cricket on his shoulders.
articles.author: Mohammad Isam

articles.title: Rachin Ravindra: The rise of New Zealand's new talisman
articles.excerpt: Born in Wellington to Indian parents, Rachin Ravindra is fast becoming the heartbeat of New Zealand cricket.
articles.content:
# The rise of Rachin Ravindra

**Rachin Ravindra** was the breakout star of the 2023 ODI World Cup, and he has only gone from strength to strength.

## A name to remember

Named after **Rahul Dravid** and **Sachin Tendulkar** - Rachin - the left-hander has lived up to the billing.

## Style

A left-hander with a flowing, wristy technique, Ravindra mixes orthodoxy with white-ball innovation. His left-arm spin provides a handy second string.

## What's next

Still only 25, Ravindra has the all-format game to rival the greats of New Zealand cricket. The 2025 Champions Trophy was another step in his evolution.

articles.title: Blazers’ Aadhav Iyer Targets USA Under-19 And Senior Team Opportunities
articles.excerpt: USACricketers.com speaks with Aadhav Iyer, a Fremont, California, native and Blazers cricketer, about his journey from youth cricket in the USA and domestic cricket in India to Min
articles.content:
_**[USACricketers.com](https://usacricketers.com/)** speaks with Aadhav Iyer, a Fremont, California, native and Blazers cricketer, about his journey from youth cricket in the USA and domestic cricket in India to Minor League Cricket, his debut experience, and his ambitions to represent the USA at the Under-19 and senior levels._  
  
My name is Aadhav Iyer. I was born in Fremont, California, where I still live. I am a first-year college student studying economics at San Jose State University. I have represented domestic teams in India, including Tamil Nadu. In the USA, I have represented the West Zone at the Under-15 level and the Blazers at the Under-19 level. I currently represent the Blazers in Minor League Cricket and at the youth level.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Aadhav Iyer, a Blazers cricketer from Fremont, California, reflects on his Minor League Cricket debut, his experience in Indian domestic cricket and his ambitions to represent the USA.**  
  
**Can you tell us about your cricketing journey and how you got started in the game?**  
My cricket journey started in the USA when I was four years old, watching my brother play with my dad. Since both of them had played cricket, I was eager to join in as well, and I discovered that I had a natural talent for the game. With the right coaching and mentoring, I flourished and progressed quickly through the older age groups, playing Under-15 cricket at 11 and Under-17 cricket at 14. I then went to India and played domestic cricket there, bringing those lessons back to the USA and eventually earning the opportunity to play in Minor League Cricket.  
  
**Can you describe the emotions you experienced when you stepped onto the field for your first Minor League Cricket match?**  
I felt a mixture of nervousness and eagerness. I was nervous about matching my skills against those of some of the established players on the team and keeping up with them, but I was also eager to prove myself on a big stage.  
  
**Was there a particular moment during your debut that stood out as especially memorable?**  
The most memorable moment of my debut was taking my first wicket with the first ball of my career. It was the wicket of my longtime friend Aryan Sidhu. It felt really satisfying to make an immediate impact.  
**  
What aspects of your game were you most satisfied with during your debut, and what would you like to improve?**  
I was not very satisfied with my overall performance, but taking the wicket was a positive takeaway. I could have contributed more with the bat and shown greater positivity in the field while supporting my teammates.  
  
**What are your personal goals for the remainder of the 2026 season, and what do you hope to contribute to your team's campaign?**  
My personal goals are to make an impact in the upcoming Atlanta Open T20 and set a good example for players trying to follow the same pathway. I also hope to contribute to my team's campaign by supporting my teammates both on and off the field and being a disciplined teammate.  
  
6\. Has your Minor League Cricket experience changed your ambitions in any way, particularly regarding Major League Cricket or opportunities to represent the USA?  
Since the introduction of MiLC and MLC, my goal has always been to play in MiLC and represent the USA Under-19 team, making a positive impact at that level. Eventually, I want to keep working hard and performing well enough to earn my way into MLC and, ultimately, the USA men's team.  
  
**What has been the biggest adjustment for you, whether in terms of playing conditions, travel, preparation, or the quality of opposition?**  
The biggest adjustment for me has been adapting to the playing conditions, as the pitches in California were very different from those I was used to playing on in India. I have never worried about the opposition because, as long as I prepare well and perform to the best of my ability, I know I can put up a good fight.  
  
**How would you describe the team environment, and what has it been like sharing the dressing room with experienced and established players?**  
The team environment is very disciplined and player-focused. Sharing the dressing room with such experienced players has been a blessing because I have picked up many little things from their daily routines, mental approach, and attitude toward the game. These lessons will also help me develop as a player.  
  
**What message would you like to share with young cricketers in the USA who are working toward making their own Minor League Cricket debut?**  
The one thing I have to say to all the young cricketers coming through this pathway is to keep persevering, no matter what happens. As Sachin Tendulkar said, “If people throw stones at you, convert them into milestones.”

articles.title: Syon Kurdekar Reflects On His Minor League Cricket Debut
articles.excerpt: My name is Syon Kurdekar. I was born in Los Gatos, California, and currently live in Fremont, California. I am a junior at John F. Kennedy High School in Fremont. I have represente
articles.content:
My name is Syon Kurdekar. I was born in Los Gatos, California, and currently live in Fremont, California. I am a junior at John F. Kennedy High School in Fremont. I have represented the Blazers at the Under-15 level, as well as the Under-15 Team in national tournament, and currently play for the East Bay Blazers. Cricket has been a major part of my life, and I have had the opportunity to compete at a high level, including representing my team nationally.  
  
**Can you tell us about your cricketing journey and how you got started in the game?**  
I started playing cricket at a young age, and over time, it grew from something I enjoyed into a passion. I spent years developing my skills through club cricket, tournaments, practice sessions, and competition against strong players. Along the way, I have been fortunate to receive recognition through Man of the Match awards, Best Batter and Best Wicketkeeper honors. Representing my team at the national level and finishing second was also a very important experience for me. Cricket has taught me discipline, patience, teamwork, and how to handle both success and setbacks.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Syon Kurdekar, who represents the East Bay Blazers, reflects on his Minor League Cricket debut, his development through youth cricket and his ambitions to reach higher levels of the game.**  
  
**Can you describe the emotions you experienced when you stepped onto the field for your first Minor League Cricket match?**  
Walking onto the field for my first Minor League Cricket match was a very special moment. I was excited but also a little nervous because I knew I was competing at a higher level against experienced players. At the same time, I felt proud because all the practice, sacrifices, and years of hard work had led to that moment. Once the game started, I focused on staying calm, trusting my preparation, and contributing to the team.  
  
**Was there a particular moment during your debut that stood out as especially memorable?**  
The entire experience of stepping onto the field for my first Minor League Cricket match was memorable. One of the biggest moments for me was realizing that I was competing at this level alongside players I had looked up to. Being part of the team environment and experiencing the intensity and professionalism of the match made my debut something I will remember for a long time.  
  
**What aspects of your game were you most satisfied with during your debut, and what would you like to improve?**  
I was most satisfied with my ability to stay composed and compete at a higher level than I had experienced before. I also learned a lot about the importance of making good decisions under pressure. Moving forward, I want to become more consistent in every aspect of my game, especially my decision-making, running between the wickets, and fielding. I want to use every opportunity to identify areas where I can improve.  
  
**What are your personal goals for the remainder of the 2026 season, and what do you hope to contribute to your team's campaign?**  
My goal for the rest of the 2026 season is to continue improving with every game and become a more reliable player for my team. I want to contribute through my performances, energy, and attitude while helping the team wherever I am needed. More than focusing on individual statistics, I want to make an impact in important moments and help my team have a successful season.  
  
**Has your Minor League Cricket experience changed your ambitions in any way, particularly regarding Major League Cricket or opportunities to represent the USA?**  
The experience has definitely motivated me to continue pursuing cricket at the highest level possible. Playing Minor League Cricket has shown me what it takes to compete professionally and given me a better understanding of the level I need to reach. It has made opportunities such as playing in Major League Cricket and potentially representing the USA feel like realistic goals that I can work toward through continued improvement, discipline, and strong performances.  
  
**What has been the biggest adjustment for you, whether in terms of playing conditions, travel, preparation, or the quality of opposition?**  
The biggest adjustment has been the overall level of professionalism and intensity. Every player is experienced and competitive, so there is very little room for mistakes. Preparation is also extremely important because you have to be ready both physically and mentally for every match. Adapting to different conditions and learning from more experienced players have been valuable parts of the experience.  
  
**How would you describe the team environment, and what has it been like sharing the dressing room with experienced and established players?**  
The team environment has been a great learning experience. Being around experienced and established players has allowed me to learn not only about cricket but also about preparation, professionalism, communication, and how to handle pressure situations. Sharing the dressing room with these players has motivated me to raise my own standards and understand what it takes to perform consistently at this level.  
**  
What message would you like to share with young cricketers in the USA who are working toward making their own Minor League Cricket debut?**  
My biggest message would be to stay patient and keep working, even when progress feels slow. Focus on improving your skills every day, and don't be afraid to learn from your mistakes. Take every opportunity to play, compete, and learn from the players around you. Most importantly, enjoy the game and stay committed to the process. If you continue putting in the work and taking every opportunity seriously, you will give yourself the best chance to reach the next level.

articles.title: Italia T10 Cricket Confirms Venice Livewires Franchise Ahead Of Rome Tournament
articles.excerpt: Pictured from left to right: Arvind Tadakamalla of Livewires Advertising, Aamir Akhtar, chairman and co-founder of Italia T10 Cricket, and TNR Mohit at the Venice Livewires franchi
articles.content:
![](/uploads/https-usacricketers-com-uploads-35ac5f59-yvvno.jpg)

**Pictured from left to right: Arvind Tadakamalla of Livewires Advertising, Aamir Akhtar, chairman and co-founder of Italia T10 Cricket, and TNR Mohit at the Venice Livewires franchise signing ceremony in Hyderabad ahead of the inaugural season in Rome.**  
  
Livewires Sporting Venture has acquired the Venice Livewires franchise ahead of the inaugural Italia T10 Cricket season, scheduled to take place in Rome from Nov. 18 to 29, 2026.  
  
The acquisition was formalized at a signing ceremony in Hyderabad, attended by Arvind Tadakamalla, managing director of Livewires Advertising Private Limited; former India cricketer MSK Prasad, who will serve as team director of Venice Livewires; professional cricketer TNR Mohit; and Aamir Akhtar, chairman and co-founder of Italia T10 Cricket.  
  
The agreement marks Livewires Sporting Venture's entry into international franchise cricket and establishes its involvement in the new Italian competition, which will feature six city-based teams competing in the 10-over format.  
  
Venice Livewires will represent Venice in the league's inaugural season, joining five other franchises in a tournament aimed at expanding the domestic cricket landscape in Italy through a franchise-based competition.  
  
Prasad's appointment as team director brings former international playing experience to the Venice franchise. His role will involve working with the team as it prepares for its debut season, although further details about the squad, coaching staff and player recruitment have not been announced.  
  
The acquisition brings together the Livewires business group's commercial interests and the league's plans to establish a franchise competition in Italy. The signing ceremony formalized the partnership between the franchise owner and the league ahead of the November tournament.  
  
Endorsed by the Italian Cricket Federation, Italia T10 will feature six city-based franchises, three of which have already been secured. The interest generated by the league’s announcement has strengthened the organizers’ confidence in its international prospects, with the Middle East identified as a potential focus for future engagement.  
  
The addition of Venice Livewires represents another step in the league's preparations for its first season. However, details regarding the complete list of participating franchises, player rosters, match schedule and tournament arrangements remain to be confirmed.  
  
T10 cricket, played over 10 overs per side, offers a shorter alternative to traditional limited-overs formats and is designed to produce results within a condensed playing window. The format has been adopted by several franchise competitions internationally, with organizers seeking to attract audiences through shorter matches.  
  
For Livewires Sporting Venture, the acquisition provides an opportunity to enter the international cricket market through a team based in Venice. For Italia T10 Cricket, securing franchise ownership ahead of the opening season is part of the process of putting its six-team competition in place.  
  
Venice Livewires are now set to make their competitive debut when the inaugural Italia T10 Cricket season begins in Rome on Nov. 18, 2026.

articles.title: Jayasuriya, Ranjane Star As USA Overcome UAE In World Cup League 2
articles.excerpt: Shubham Ranjane took four wickets for 39 runs and hit an unbeaten 14 in USA win over United Arab Emirates by five wickets in the ICC CWC League 2 in Dallas. File photo courtesy of
articles.content:
![](/uploads/https-usacricketers-com-uploads-f2ec34e9-psywi.jpg)

**Shubham Ranjane took four wickets for 39 runs and hit an unbeaten 14 in USA win over United Arab Emirates by five wickets in the ICC CWC League 2 in Dallas. File photo courtesy of ICC**  
**[  
Scorecard](https://www.icc-cricket.com/tournaments/icc-cricket-world-cup-league-2/matches/275015/usa-vs-united-arab-emirates)**  
The United States defeated the United Arab Emirates by five wickets in the ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup League 2, chasing a target of 214 in 38.4 overs at Grand Prairie Cricket Stadium in Dallas on Sunday, October 11.  
  
Shehan Jayasuriya scored 83 and Shubham Ranjane took four wickets to lead the USA’s effort. The hosts finished at 214 for five after bowling out the UAE for 213 in 46.3 overs, securing the victory with 68 balls remaining.  
  
Ranjane was named Player of the Match after taking four wickets for 39 runs in 10 overs and contributing an unbeaten 14 from 21 balls during the chase.  
  
After winning the toss and electing to field, the USA struck early when Ranjane dismissed Tanish Suri for one. Adeeb Usmani made 12 before falling to Nosthush Kenjige, leaving the UAE at 33 for two in 11.4 overs.  
  
Muhammad Shahdad and Harpreet Singh Bhatia then steadied the innings with a third-wicket partnership that took the score to 131. Shahdad anchored the recovery with 79 from 105 balls, including seven fours and two sixes, while Bhatia scored 48 off 53 deliveries, hitting five fours and a six.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Shehan Jayasuriya top scored for USA with 83, which came off 95 deliveries and included eight fours and a six. File photo courtesy of ICC**  
  
Hassan Khan broke the stand by dismissing Bhatia, and Saurabh Netravalkar removed Rahul Chopra for 20. Ranjane then struck repeatedly to prevent the UAE from building another substantial partnership. He dismissed Basil Hameed for six, Shahdad and Akshdeep Nath for two, finishing with four wickets.  
  
Netravalkar claimed three for 23 from 9.3 overs, while Jasdeep Singh and Kenjige took one wicket apiece. Awais Ali Shah remained unbeaten on 24 from 26 balls, but the UAE lost its final three wickets for 11 runs to be dismissed for 213.  
  
The USA’s chase began poorly when captain Monank Patel fell for a duck in the second over to Muhammad Arfan. Smit Patel and Jayasuriya rebuilt the innings, adding 75 for the second wicket before Smit was dismissed for 25 from 45 balls.  
  
Jayasuriya continued to control the chase, reaching his half-century from 65 deliveries. He struck eight fours and a six in his 95-ball innings, providing the foundation for the home side’s pursuit.  
  
Sanjay Krishnamurthy contributed 28 from 36 balls in a 65-run partnership with Jayasuriya, taking the USA to 140 before Muhammad Arfan dismissed him. Milind Kumar then accelerated the scoring, hitting two fours and two sixes in his 23-ball 27. He and Jayasuriya added 44 runs before Arfan removed Kumar, and Jayasuriya followed for 83 at 189 for five.  
  
Arfan finished with three for 38 from 10 overs, but the UAE could not force another breakthrough. Ranjane and Hassan Khan, who scored 15 not out from 10 balls, completed the chase with an unbroken partnership.

articles.title: Monank Patel’s 108 Leads USA To Four-wicket Win Over Namibia In League 2
articles.excerpt: Skipper Monank Patel struck 108 from 100 balls as USA beat Namibia by four wickets in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2. File photo by Shiek Mohamed Scorecard The United States ch
articles.content:
![](/uploads/https-usacricketers-com-uploads-cf5a3779-8pszz.jpg)

**Skipper Monank Patel struck 108 from 100 balls as USA beat Namibia by four wickets in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2. File photo by Shiek Mohamed**  
  
**[Scorecard](https://www.icc-cricket.com/tournaments/icc-cricket-world-cup-league-2/matches/275013/usa-vs-namibia#scorecard)**  
The United States chased down Namibia’s 298 for 9 with seven balls to spare, winning by four wickets at Grand Prairie Cricket Stadium in Dallas on Wednesday to strengthen their position in the ICC Cricket World Cup League 2, 2023-27.  
  
Monank Patel led the chase with a composed 108 from 100 balls, while Shehan Jayasuriya added 74 from 75 as the USA reached 299 for 6 in 48.5 overs. Patel was named Player of the Match for his century, which included 14 fours and came at a strike rate of 108.00.  
  
Namibia, sent in first, recovered from a difficult start through Michael van Lingen and Gerhard Erasmus. Van Lingen scored 124 from 121 balls, hitting 11 fours, while Erasmus made 76 from 45 balls with nine fours and three sixes. Their efforts helped Namibia recover from 24 for 2 and build a competitive total.  
  
Van Lingen brought up his century from 94 balls, having earlier reached 50 in 50 deliveries. His partnership with Louren Steenkamp was particularly important, producing 100 runs from 107 balls after Namibia had lost two early wickets. Steenkamp contributed 30 from 55 balls.  
  
Erasmus then accelerated the innings, reaching his half-century from just 27 balls. His 100-run partnership with Van Lingen came from 67 deliveries and pushed Namibia beyond 200 before the visitors lost wickets regularly in the final 10 overs. Namibia added 74 runs during the last powerplay but lost six wickets, finishing on 298 for 9.  
  
Saurabh Netravalkar, Milind Kumar and Ehsan Adil took one, one and four wickets respectively for the USA. Adil was the pick of the bowlers, finishing with 4 for 41 from eight overs. Shehan Jayasuriya also claimed three wickets for 30 runs.  
  
The USA began their reply steadily, with Smit Patel and Monank Patel putting on 96 for the opening wicket. Smit made 50 from 62 balls before Jan Nicol Loftie Eaton dismissed him in the 18th over. Monank continued to anchor the chase, reaching his half-century from 58 balls and his century from 92.  
  
Jayasuriya provided the ideal support, forming a 100-run partnership with Monank from 89 balls. He reached his fifty from 50 deliveries before falling for 74 with the USA 232 for 4.  
  
Although Namibia claimed three wickets during the final powerplay, the USA remained in control. Milind Kumar made 18 from 13 balls before falling at 282, while Shubham Ranjane and Harmeet Singh completed the chase with unbeaten scores of six and 12 respectively.  
  
The result gives the USA another important victory in the League 2 campaign, while Namibia will be left to assess the missed opportunity after posting nearly 300 but failing to defend it.

**Freedom Flyers won the inaugural tournament earlier this year.  
  
We are disappointed to announce that the 2nd edition of the American Women's Cricket Support Group tournament has been postponed due to persistent rain, thunderstorms, and hurricanes. We value the safety of all our players, officials, and families, and made this decision with their safety in mind.  
  
The same teams will compete in the same format once we finalize the details. Mother Nature gave us a break for now, but we’ll be back later.  
  
GROVELAND, Fla.** — The American Women’s Cricket Support Group (AWCSG) announces the second edition of its Women’s Premier T25 Cricket Tournament, taking place October 9–12, 2026, at the Orlando Cricket Ground in Groveland, Florida. Two matches will be played each day, culminating in the finals on Monday, October 12.  
  
Building on the inaugural tournament held in April this year, the second edition expands the competition from three teams to four: American Titans, Freedom Flyers, Patriots, and Liberty. Each team will carry a roster of 13 players, with the tournament format allowing eleven players to bowl and twelve to bat.  
  
The 52 players, aged 15 to 35, were selected in an August draft from a pool of more than 60 cricketers resident in the United States. The pool included current USA under-19 and senior women’s national team players, alongside players drawn from the USA tier system.  
  
Each team has been assigned a head coach. The USA under-19 and senior women’s national team players have been distributed among the four teams, with the skill sets of all 52 drafted players considered to form balanced, competitive squads.  
  
“The matches involving players between the ages of 15 and 35 will be live-streamed, involving six cameras and a broadcast commentary crew,” said Suresh Vallabhaneni, an AWCSG committee member, adding, “We have increased the number of overs from the traditional 20 to 25, to allow greater participation by the players.”  
  
The four-day tournament will bring established national team talent and emerging domestic players together, showcasing the depth of women’s cricket talent in the United States and giving players an additional opportunity to compete and develop.

**• Dates:** October 9–12, 2026, with two matches each day  
**• Finals:** Monday, October 12  
**• Venue:** Orlando Cricket Ground, Groveland, Florida  
**• Teams:** American Titans, Freedom Flyers, Patriots, and Liberty  
**• Players:** 52 across four 13-player rosters

articles.title: Rayyan Ketekar On His Minor League Cricket Debut And Future Goals
articles.excerpt: Rayyan Ketekar was born and raised in the Bay Area and is a sophomore at Santa Clara University, where he is pursuing a major in mathematics and a minor in Management Information S
articles.content:
Rayyan Ketekar was born and raised in the Bay Area and is a sophomore at Santa Clara University, where he is pursuing a major in mathematics and a minor in Management Information Systems. He has represented the Bay Area and Santa Clara Cricket Club and most recently made his Minor League Cricket debut with the East Bay Blazers.

  
**1\. Can you tell us about your cricketing journey and how you got started in the game?**  
Cricket sparked my interest in sports after watching the 2017 Champions Trophy. After learning the basics and playing my first couple of games, I believed I could pursue the sport professionally. I later progressed through the USA Youth Cricket pathway while also taking part in numerous tournaments domestically and abroad, including in Australia, the United Kingdom and South Africa.  
![](/uploads/https-usacricketers-com-uploads-9c810001-3jhk2.jpg)

**Rayyan Ketekar made his Minor League Cricket debut for the East Bay Blazers in 2026 after progressing through the USA Youth Cricket pathway and playing internationally.**  
  
**2\. Can you describe the emotions you experienced when you stepped onto the field for your first Minor League Cricket match?**  
It was a moment of pride for me. Stepping onto the field reflected my hard work, resilience and consistent performances both domestically and abroad. Before and during the match, I made sure to approach the game with the mindset that I belonged on this stage and that success would come as long as I stuck to the process, worked hard and remained patient.  
  
**3\. Was there a particular moment during your debut that stood out as especially memorable?**  
As a team, we went into my debut game with the mindset that we would fight hard to secure a spot in the playoffs. The final five overs of the Blazers' bowling innings were nothing short of a potential miracle. With a tough task of defending 11 runs in five overs with six wickets still to take, I knew my job was to keep racking up dot balls and putting pressure on the set batters. The reward was a debut wicket in my first MiLC spell and a rapid lower-order collapse that followed, courtesy of my teammates.  
  
Despite the loss, the East Bay Blazers managed to take an important match into the final over. I can proudly walk away knowing that my two overs hindered the opposition's qualification chances.  
  
**4\. What aspects of your game were you most satisfied with during your debut, and what would you like to improve?**  
I was satisfied with the lengths I hit while bowling and with not conceding extras given the tight match situation. This opportunity provided me with a lot of input that I can take back to the drawing board and use to prepare for next season. I want to focus more on variations, develop a consistent strength-and-conditioning plan suited to my role, and improve my fielding.  
  
**5\. What are your personal goals for the remainder of the 2026 season, and what do you hope to contribute to your team's campaign?**  
My goals for the rest of the year are to get stronger, bowl faster, work on my power-hitting and improve my fitness. I am looking forward to taking more wickets and bowling impactful spells to help the East Bay Blazers win back the West Division Championship and compete for the title in 2027.  
  
**6\. Has your Minor League Cricket experience changed your ambitions in any way, particularly regarding Major League Cricket or opportunities to represent the USA?**  
This experience has given me exposure to a high level of competitive cricket. Looking ahead, I aim to make an impact in Minor League Cricket and work my way toward the USA men's team, Major League Cricket and other professional franchise leagues.  
  
**7\. What has been the biggest adjustment for you, whether in terms of playing conditions, travel, preparation or the quality of opposition?**  
The biggest adjustment to my routine was the depth and quality of my training, especially leading up to the Minor League games. Knowing the physical demands of cricket at the men's level, I made sure to align and schedule my gym sessions, academy coaching, one-on-one sessions and matches accordingly. This allowed me to effectively manage my workload and benefit from the open-net training camps conducted by the East Bay Blazers to prepare for the tournament.  
  
**8\. How would you describe the team environment, and what has it been like sharing the dressing room with experienced and established players?**  
I'm grateful to be around people who have so much knowledge to share about the sport, especially players who have participated in Major League Cricket and represented national teams. They are role models for me and for the youth at the academy who aspire to become great cricketers.  
  
They are calm and composed athletes who relentlessly back the team and inspire us to put in the hard yards. The dugout culture is very welcoming and disciplined.  
  
**9\. What message would you like to share with young cricketers in the USA who are working toward making their own Minor League Cricket debut?**  
My advice to the youth: Cricket is a game of highs and lows. If you put in the work, it will pay off in the long run. Above all, enjoy the game and stay patient.

articles.title: USA Chase 331 As Milind Kumar Hits Unbeaten 116 Against UAE
articles.excerpt: Milind Kumar struck an unbeaten 116 as USA chased down UAE's 330 for eight to seal a six-wicket victory in the ICC CWC League 2 in Dallas. File photo by Shiek Mohamed DALLAS — Mili
articles.content:
![](/uploads/https-usacricketers-com-uploads-aff602f0-octfd.jpg)

**Milind Kumar struck an unbeaten 116 as USA chased down UAE's 330 for eight to seal a six-wicket victory in the ICC CWC League 2 in Dallas. File photo by Shiek Mohamed****  
  
DALLAS** — Milind Kumar struck an unbeaten 116 from 84 balls as the United States chased down 331 to beat the United Arab Emirates by six wickets in the ICC CWC League 2, 2023-27 at Grand Prairie Cricket Stadium on Oct. 5, 2026.  
  
USA reached 332 for four in 48.5 overs, with Kumar and Shubham Ranjane completing the chase with seven balls to spare. Ranjane finished unbeaten on 57 from 49 balls, while the pair added an unbeaten 160 for the fifth wicket to turn a challenging chase into a comfortable finish. Kumar was named Player of the Match.  
  
UAE, having been sent in, made 330 for eight from their 50 overs. Tanish Suri and Adeeb Usmani put on 50 from 57 balls during the opening phase before Usmani was dismissed for 36. Suri continued to anchor the innings, reaching his half-century from 57 balls, and eventually made 78 from 78 balls with 10 fours and two sixes.  
  
Muhammad Shahdad provided the main acceleration in the middle and late overs. He reached 103 from 101 balls before completing a 114-run innings from 107 deliveries, hitting nine fours and three sixes. His dismissal at 295 for seven came in the 48th over, but Basil Hameed's unbeaten 24 from 11 balls, including three sixes, helped UAE finish at 330.  
  
Harmeet Singh was USA's most successful bowler, taking four wickets for 65 runs from his 10 overs. Saurabh Netravalkar, Ehsan Adil, Jasdeep Singh and Shubham Ranjane claimed one wicket apiece.  
  
USA's chase began briskly but was interrupted by regular wickets. Smit Patel made 27 from 22 balls before falling at 38, while Shehan Jayasuriya was dismissed for nine with the score on 60. Monank Patel then made 55 from 62 balls before UAE removed him when the score was 134. Saiteja Mukkamalla, who reached his half-century from 52 balls, made 56 before falling at 172 for four.  
  
With USA four down, Kumar and Ranjane took control. Their first 50-run stand came from 49 balls, followed by a 100-run partnership from 75 deliveries. The pair then brought up 150 together from 107 balls. Kumar reached 50 from 39 balls and his century from 76, while Ranjane completed his half-century from 47 balls.  
  
Kumar's 116 included seven fours and five sixes, while Ranjane's 57 contained two fours and three sixes. UAE's bowlers struggled to contain the final partnership, with Ibrar Ahmad conceding 82 from nine overs and Aayan Afzal Khan 72 from 10.

articles.title: Clifford S. Hinds Remembered For More Than 50 Years Of Service To New York Cricket
articles.excerpt: 1. Clifford Hinds, a longtime cricket administrator whose service helped shape New York and Tri-State cricket for more than five decades. File photo by Shiek Mohamed By Rahul Sharm
articles.content:
1.  ![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Clifford Hinds, a longtime cricket administrator whose service helped shape New York and Tri-State cricket for more than five decades. File photo by Shiek Mohamed  
      
    By Rahul Sharma | [Photo Gallery](https://usacricketers.com/gallery-detail.php?slug=Remembering+Clifford+Hinds)**  
    **A Commemorative Lifetime Tribute  
    A Lifetime Dedicated to Cricket**  
    Celebrating the life, service and enduring legacy of Mr. Clifford S. Hinds  
    _“He did not merely serve cricket. He helped carry its traditions, strengthen its institutions, and open the way for generations to follow.”_  
      
    **The Measure Of A Life  
    More Than a Cricket Administrator**  
    _A legacy measured not in titles, but in service, sacrifice and lives touched._  
    There are lives that are remembered because of the offices they held, the honors they received, or the records they left behind. And then there are lives remembered for something deeper: the people they encouraged, the institutions they strengthened, the opportunities they created, and the values they quietly passed from one generation to the next.  
      
    Mr. Clifford S. Hinds belonged to that rare second category. For more than half a century, his name became intertwined with the story of cricket in New York and the wider Tri-State region. His contribution was not confined to a committee room, a tournament calendar, or a single era. It was woven into the continuity of the game itself.  
      
    _“His contribution was not a chapter in New York cricket. It became part of the thread that connected one generation of the game to another.”_  
      
    To call him simply a cricket administrator would be to understate the breadth of his service. He was a mentor, organizer, bridge-builder, advocate for youth, guardian of cricketing tradition, and, above all, a man who understood that institutions survive only when committed people are prepared to serve them faithfully.  
      
    **A Life Intertwined With the Game**  
    For Mr. Hinds, cricket was never merely a contest of bat and ball. It was community. It was discipline. It was heritage. It was fellowship. It was an avenue through which people from different backgrounds could meet on equal ground and share a common language.  
      
    He knew that every match seen by spectators rested upon countless unseen acts of responsibility: planning, organizing, communicating, mediating, mentoring and preparing. He became one of those dependable figures who performed that work not for applause, but because the game mattered.  
    ![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Hinds (left), with other cricket New York cricket administrators. File photo by Shiek Mohamed**  
      
    **Half A Century Of Commitment  
    A Builder of New York Cricket**  
    The game endures because some people choose to build beyond themselves.  
    More than 50 years of service is not simply a span of time. It is a measure of constancy. It means remaining committed while players retire, administrators change, organizations evolve, generations come of age, and the landscape of the sport is transformed.  
      
    Across those decades, Mr. Hinds represented continuity. He belonged to the generation of community cricket leaders who understood that passion alone was not enough. Cricket needed structure. It needed stewardship. It needed experienced hands willing to resolve difficulties, preserve relationships, sustain competition, and protect the interests of the game beyond any single season.  
      
    **The Foundation Behind the Scoreboard**  
    The public sees runs, wickets, centuries and trophies. Yet none of those moments can exist without the foundation beneath them. Someone must convene the meetings. Someone must organize the competition. Someone must answer the difficult telephone call. Someone must reconcile competing interests. Someone must keep the door open for the next club, the next team and the next young player.  
    _  
    “The strongest pillars of cricket are often the people whose names never appear on a scorecard.”_  
      
    Mr. Hinds was one of those pillars. His service reflected a conviction that cricket was worth protecting not only for those playing today, but also for those who had not yet discovered the game.  
      
    **The Most Precious Gift: Time**  
    Of everything he gave to cricket, perhaps the most valuable was the one thing no person can recover once it is spent: time. Evenings became meetings. Weekends became tournaments. Seasons became years. Years became decades.  
      
    That sacrifice cannot be summarized in a statistic. There is no official record for the hours spent listening, advising, planning, encouraging, mediating and showing up when the game needed leadership. Yet those hours are precisely where the true scale of his contribution can be found.  
    ![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Hinds (far right) with members of Cricket 4 Change, an English organization dedicated to supporting disadvantaged children, during the group’s visit to New York in 2010. File photo by Shiek Mohamed.  
    **  
    **The Future He Helped Protect  
    A Champion for Youth and Community**  
    _Because the greatest administrators do not merely preserve the present—they prepare the future._  
      
    **Investing in the Next Generation**  
    One of the most meaningful dimensions of Mr. Hinds’s legacy was his commitment to youth cricket and the development of future generations. He understood that the survival of any sport depends upon whether young people are welcomed, encouraged and given a genuine opportunity to belong.  
      
    Youth cricket is not simply about producing the next batsman, bowler or captain. At its best, it teaches discipline, patience, responsibility, teamwork, humility, resilience and respect. It gives young people a place to test themselves, to fail and recover, to compete and still shake hands, and to discover that character matters as much as talent.  
      
    _“When you invest in a young cricketer, you are not only developing a player. You are helping shape the person who may one day carry the game forward.”_  
      
    By supporting youth cricket, Mr. Hinds invested in more than the next fixture. He invested in the future custodians of the sport.  
      
    **Cricket as a Bridge Between Communities**  
    New York’s cricket story is inseparable from its diversity. Caribbean, South Asian, English, African and other cricketing traditions have all found expression on its grounds. Different accents, different histories and different customs have met at the same crease.  
      
    Mr. Hinds understood the unifying power of the game. Cricket could preserve heritage while also building new friendships. It could connect generations within families and create bonds across communities. In that sense, his service to cricket was also service to the social fabric around it.  
    ![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Umpire Hinds, another reflection of his lifelong commitment to the game. File photo by Shiek Mohamed**  
      
    **Leadership Without the Spotlight**  
    The truest measure of leadership often appears when there is no audience. It is found in the difficult conversation, the patient explanation, the quiet encouragement, the willingness to remain after others have left, and the decision to serve even when recognition never comes. That kind of leadership formed an important part of Mr. Hinds’s legacy.  
      
    **The Record Beyond Statistics  
    The Scorecard Cricket Cannot Create**  
    _Some contributions are too large to be captured by numbers._  
    Cricket is a game that records almost everything. Runs. Wickets. Averages. Partnerships. Centuries. Victories. But there is no official scorecard for service.  
      
    There is no column for decades of loyalty. No average for wisdom shared. No statistic for a disagreement resolved before it fractured a community. No boundary count for opportunities created. No official record for the youngster encouraged to return after a difficult day.  
      
    “If cricket kept a scorecard of service, Mr. Hinds’s numbers would be measured not in runs, but in years given, people helped and generations connected.”  
      
    **A Bridge Between Eras**  
    To remain involved in cricket across more than half a century is to become a witness to history. Mr. Hinds saw the game through changing generations, changing organizations and changing expectations. With time, experience becomes more than memory; it becomes institutional wisdom.  
      
    History does not live only in archives, photographs and minutes of meetings. Sometimes history lives in people: in what they remember, what they teach, what they preserve, and what they refuse to let disappear.  
    ![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Hinds (left) was instrumental with the pioneer launch of women's cricket in New York, which led to a national championship by 2011. File photo by Shiek Mohamed  
      
    A Custodian, Not an Owner**  
    The finest administrators understand that cricket belongs to no individual. We inherit the game from those who came before us, hold it in trust for a period of time, and then pass it onward. The duty is not to possess the game, but to leave it stronger.  
      
    Mr. Hinds’s long service embodied that idea of stewardship. His legacy asks every administrator a simple but demanding question: When your own innings of service is complete, will the game be better because you were here?  
      
    **The Meaning of Legacy**  
    Titles fade. Committees change. Trophies gather dust. Legacy is different. Legacy survives in habits, standards, memories, opportunities and people. It is carried by the young player who becomes a coach, the volunteer who becomes an administrator, and the community that continues to gather around the game year after year.  
      
    **In Lasting Tribute  
    A Standing Ovation for an Extraordinary Innings**  
    _His innings is complete. His influence remains._  
    Cricket gives us a language uniquely suited to remembering a life of service. Every innings eventually ends. But some innings are remembered not because of a number beside a name, but because of what they meant to everyone who witnessed them.  
      
    His runs were the opportunities he helped create for others.  
      
    His partnerships were the relationships he strengthened across the cricket community.  
      
    His boundaries were the obstacles overcome through patience, leadership and persistence.  
      
    His centuries were the generations that continued playing because people like him refused to let the game fade.  
      
    By that measure, Mr. Clifford S. Hinds played an extraordinary innings—one that extended across more than half a century and reached far beyond the boundary.  
      
    **The Pavilion Rises**  
    There is a moment in cricket when a player who has given everything begins the walk back toward the pavilion. Teammates rise. Spectators stand. Even opponents may pause to acknowledge an innings worthy of respect.  
      
    For Mr. Hinds, that standing ovation belongs not to a single performance, but to a lifetime: to the years given freely, the responsibilities carried, the communities strengthened, the youth encouraged, and the unwavering belief that cricket in New York deserved both a proud present and a secure future.  
      
    _“The greatest tribute we can offer is not merely to remember his name, but to continue the values his service represented.”_  
      
    To honor his legacy is to protect the game, invest in youth, strengthen our institutions, respect those who came before us, and serve with the understanding that cricket is larger than any one individual.

articles.title: ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup 2027 Schedule Announced As Ticket Ballot Opens
articles.excerpt: The ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup 2027 will begin on October 2, 2027, with South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia set to host a 14-team tournament featuring 57 matches across 12 venues.
articles.content:
The ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup 2027 will begin on October 2, 2027, with South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia set to host a 14-team tournament featuring 57 matches across 12 venues.  
  
The schedule was unveiled in Cape Town on October 2, 2026, marking the one-year countdown to the tournament and opening the ticket ballot for fans. The competition will run through November 21, when the final will be played in Johannesburg.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)  
Defending champions Australia and 2023 finalists India will headline the opening weekend when they meet at Newlands Cricket Ground in Cape Town on October 7. New Zealand will face hosts South Africa in Tshwane on October 8, while India and Pakistan will renew their rivalry at Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg on October 10.  
  
The opening round will also see Afghanistan play Pakistan in Centurion on October 8, while England take on Bangladesh in Windhoek. Zimbabwe will return to the men's World Cup after a 12-year absence when they face Qualifier-A at Queen's Sports Club in Bulawayo on October 9. South Africa will begin their campaign against New Zealand in Cape Town on the same day.  
  
Zimbabwe will later host India at the Mosi-oa-Tunya Stadium in Victoria Falls in Match 33, taking the tournament to one of the country's most prominent tourist destinations.  
  
The competition will start with a Super Series in Namibia involving the three lowest-ranked of the 14 qualified teams. They will play a round-robin competition, with the winner advancing to the Group Stage.  
  
The 12-team Group Stage will then be divided into two groups of six. Group A will comprise India, Australia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and Qualifier A, while Group B will feature New Zealand, South Africa, Sri Lanka, England, Bangladesh and Qualifier B.  
  
Each group will play a single round robin. The top three teams from each group, along with the highest-ranked fourth-placed team across the two groups, will advance to the Super 7.  
  
The Super 7 will feature seven teams playing a complete single round robin, producing 21 matches. India, Australia, Pakistan, England, New Zealand, South Africa and Sri Lanka have been pre-seeded into designated positions, although a qualifying team can take the position of a seeded side it finishes above.  
  
The top four teams after the Super 7 will advance to the semi-finals. The first-placed team will meet fourth, while second will face third. The semi-finals are scheduled for Cape Town on November 17 and Tshwane on November 18, with the final in Johannesburg on November 21.  
  
Ten teams had secured direct qualification by September 30, 2026, including hosts South Africa and Zimbabwe. The remaining four places will be decided through the ICC Men's Cricket World Cup Qualifier 2027. The qualifier winner will enter the Group Stage, while the second-, third- and fourth-placed teams will enter the Super Series.  
  
The tournament's schedule now provides the competitive pathway through to the final, while the ticket ballot remains open until 11:59 p.m. SAST on November 21, 2026.

articles.title: ICC Introduces New Rules For Batters, Balls And Fielding
articles.excerpt: The ICC has introduced revised Playing Conditions covering time-wasting, cricket-ball specifications, fielding regulations and a trial allowing pink balls in daytime Test matches.
articles.content:
![](/uploads/https-usacricketers-com-uploads-753abf00-k6u8y.jpg)

**The ICC has introduced revised Playing Conditions covering time-wasting, cricket-ball specifications, fielding regulations and a trial allowing pink balls in daytime Test matches. File photo by Shiek Mohamed**  
  
The International Cricket Council has introduced a series of changes to its Playing Conditions aimed at addressing time-wasting, standardizing cricket-ball specifications and clarifying several fielding regulations.  
  
The changes apply to international series beginning on October 1, 2026, or later, while series already in progress will continue under the previous regulations. The updated Playing Conditions for men's and women's cricket across all formats incorporate changes to the MCC Laws of Cricket that come into effect on October 1.  
  
One of the most significant changes in men's cricket concerns batters who are not ready to face the next delivery within the prescribed time. A first offense will result in a warning, followed by a final warning for a second offense. A third and each subsequent offense will result in five penalty runs being awarded to the fielding side. Code of Conduct provisions may also be applied in cases of repeated offenses.  
  
The ICC has also introduced tighter specifications for the size and weight of balls used in women's international cricket. Previously, manufacturers have at times produced a single ball for women's and junior cricket. The revised regulations establish three distinct size and weight specifications for men's, women's and junior cricket.  
  
Several fielding-related provisions have been clarified. An overthrow is now defined as an attempt to direct the ball towards the stumps to prevent runs or effect a run-out. A misfield, whether an attempt to stop the ball or pass it to another fielder, does not constitute an overthrow.  
  
Umpires will also have greater discretion in determining when a ball is "finally settled", a provision that can be particularly significant on the final delivery of a close match. The ball does not necessarily have to be in the bowler's or wicketkeeper's hands to be considered settled.  
  
For run-outs and stumpings, a fielder must have complete control of the ball for it to be considered held. Simply touching the ball with a hand as it breaks the stumps will not constitute holding it.  
  
In Test cricket, a trial will allow pink balls to be used in daytime matches by mutual agreement to reduce the loss of play because of bad light. The decision must be made before the Test begins and, once agreed, applies for the entire match. A switch between red and pink balls after the match has started will not be permitted.  
  
Another Test change means the final over of the day's play will not automatically end when a wicket falls if the over remains incomplete and conditions allow play to continue.  
  
In ODIs and T20Is, the changes include a fixed 15-minute T20I interval, which can be reduced to 10 minutes when playing time has been lost. The "Head Coach or their designate" may enter the field during drinks intervals, while the leg-side wide trial has been made a permanent part of the ODI and T20I Playing Conditions.  
  
ICC Men's Cricket Committee chair Sourav Ganguly said the changes were designed to address the needs of the modern game while maintaining consistency and integrity.  
  
ICC General Manager – Events and Operations Gaurav Saxena described the process as collaborative, with discussions focused on evolving the Playing Conditions while preserving clarity and integrity.  
  
The revised regulations will govern international series beginning from October 1 and are intended to provide greater consistency in match administration across formats.
