articles.title: A Tribute To Clifford S. Hinds
articles.excerpt: By Sham Ali (Cosmos Cricket Club) | Photo Gallery Clifford S. Hinds -- jovial, gentle, pragmatic and purposeful; a magnanimous man whom merged many wide-ranging attributes across a
articles.content:
**By Sham Ali (Cosmos Cricket Club) | [Photo Gallery](https://usacricketers.com/gallery-detail.php?slug=Remembering+Clifford+Hinds)**  
Clifford S. Hinds -- jovial, gentle, pragmatic and purposeful; a magnanimous man whom merged many wide-ranging attributes across an accomplished life -- died on September 21 in New Jersey, four days shy of his 84th birthday.  A man with a decorated record of service to cricket as a player, coach, and administrator, whose pride and joy was birthing the United States of America’s first women’s cricket team in 2003.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Clifford Hinds (center) stands with Krish Prasad at Canarsie Park at the New York Region vs. Atlantic Region game.** **Photo by Sham Ali**  
  
Saddened is a word tossed around with abbreviated syllables these days in an end-of-season for elder statesmen.  The meaning often gets lost as it travels through the airwaves in a society of varied tongues and countless variables with a half-life of one minute, but in the Metropolitan Cricket League (MCL) the loss is real, the feelings are real, the brotherhood is real, knitted together in decades of genuine friendship, decency and an unwavering respect for each other.  Real, for a man who reigned large and left an indelible impression on the MCL -- a place that he loved and called home for almost four decades.  The life of Clifford Hinds was one that fully justified any accolade bestowed upon this son of Jamaican soil.  One of the few fanatical cricket students, consistent and disciplined, a dedicated club cricketer, and an astute administrator.  Hinds found far wider acclaim as a learned student of cricket, whose scholarly analysis of the cricketer’s consciousness informed every word he spoke.  Behind it all was a tormented soul, one that was eternally restless in his quest for a more structurally sound environment for the sport.  That was the irrevocable union that fused cricketers with the game, one that defined them and a pursuit that consumed their lives since they were teenagers.  
  
Few have been more willing to talk about cricket, or any sport, and wrestled as evocatively as Clifford Hinds, and bold enough to challenge the norms.  A gentler, more sensitive observer of the game has rarely drawn breath.  At a time when judgments are so often harsh and the accent is on serious analysis of techniques and tactics in a cluttered electronic world, Clifford Hinds’ cricketing figures were necessarily delivered with ‘that West Indies’ bias of flare and flamboyance - even when they were happily presented as flawed characters, they were all the more magnificent.  
  
Many have crossed this path before and many more will do so, but few will be able to ‘fit the shoe’ of Clifford S. Hinds.  The United States of America cricket fraternity and particularly the New York Metropolitan Cricket League have lost a giant.  Clifford Hinds was born in St. Andrew, Jamaica.  He attended St. Mary’s Elementary School, St. George’s College and Dinthill Technical High School before attending Mico Teacher’s College and subsequently worked for the government first as a teacher and then as a youth club organizer before he migrated to the USA.  
  
A dedicated and hard-working administrator who never gave up on an opportunity to promote cricket, and through it all he gave of himself, decades of unselfish sacrifice for the cause.  He was elected president of the MCL in 1996 after serving as vice-president under another stalwart of the MCL, Clement ‘Busta’ Lawrence.  Hinds was instrumental in this writer’s involvement in the MCL administration and the New York Region (NYR).  Prior to him being elected MCL President, I received a call from Hinds to have a meeting, and he inquired whether I wanted to run for the position of corresponding secretary, actually, he insisted on incorporating the ‘young blood’, and the rest is history as his understudy.  He urged me to pick up the mantle after he decided to end his tenure in 2001 due to health issues, but the MCL had more capable personalities, and Mascelles Bailey fitted that leadership position perfectly, and I remained as the corresponding secretary.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Hinds at a USACA trial at Woodley Park in California.** **Photo by Sham Ali**  
  
The MCL was on firm footing and when Hinds was elected the 26th President, however, he had a vision to further enhance the League’s prestige.  He had managed the MCL team in the NYR inter-league competition.  The MCL team was a powerhouse with the likes of Ashmul Ali (captain), Alfie Walker (vice-captain, wicketkeeper), Ken Williams (captained two seasons), Compton Adams, Ed Lewis, Trevor Walke (captained one season), Hazrat Amin, Clem Thompson, Zamin Amin, Sham Ali, Terry Hastoo, Saheed Amin, Raldo Brissett, R. ‘Jumbo’ Hamilton, Norris Gordon, Dwight Meikle, Ray Winter, Harriman Joseph, Richard Staple, Ram Goolsarran, Herbert Carrington, John Slocombe,  Devon Campbell, Eswart ‘Cobla’ Thomas, Robert Henriques, Ballister McLiesh, Everton Mattis, and Roy ‘Country’ Ricketts.  I can still hear Hinds’ proud reverberations in his familiar Jamaican tone, “cho them other leagues couldn’t touch us.”  The MCL won the Inter-League competition eight times between 1989 through 1999, including seven consecutive years (1989--1995) under his management and executive leadership.  
  
He proceeded to champion his cause as an educator with a love for sports in his early years.  Despite myriad challenges, he felt that an investment in the youths could deliver massive returns -- the youth program for the NYR henceforth became his vision.  The program started with the MCL where he solicited the expertise of Ashmul Ali to pool the youth resources of the League.  The MCL youth team was a solid group managed by Hinds and coached by Ashmul Ali and captained by Mark Baker with Barrington Bartley, Kyron Andrews, Sunesh Wazid, Willy Charles, Ricky Kissoon, Nalburn Whittaker, Andrae Hooper, Nico Cyrus, Orlando Baker, Dennis Evans, Clement Walsh, Arosh Mataraarachchige, Omar Wright, Andrew Allen, and Keeble Thomas.  
  
Hinds subsequently approached Krish Persaud – the then Eastern American Cricket League (EACA) President and NYR Director – to forge a youth program in the NYR with the primary goal of furthering the development of cricket in the NYR by getting the youths involved in cricket via an inter-league youth competition.  The MCL team was well organized, as well as the EACA; however, the other five leagues struggled.  The program gained some traction for a few years with the MCL and EACA as the driving forces, but NY cricket never failed in its deliverance despite lack of interest from the other five leagues.  Nevertheless, the program remained active with the NYR youth team competing against the other regions.  
  
After exiting the presidency of the MCL, Hinds later became active in the NYR, and in 2003 he embarked on another bold adventurous and defining vision -- a women’s cricket team was conceived and pioneered by none other than Clifford Hinds.  He appeared infatuated in his relentless pursuit to introduce women to cricket in the US, it underpinned the importance of diversification and changed forever the general complexion of the game in the United States.  Hinds pooled resources from near, far and wide while he wrestled with the challenges to get the cricket leagues and other regions to recognize the necessity for women’s cricket in the US.  This effort, though with its roots in New York, began to gain momentum and grew wings across the length and breadth of the United States.  It was a challenge for this “soldier” but Hinds, as focused as he was, and as judicious a student of the game, he championed this cause with reckless abandon!  It was the beginning of a story that will only add volumes of pages to the opening chapter in US cricket as the years rolled by, and indeed, it remained perhaps the single most significant achievement for the sport in the United States for the last five decades.  The blossoming of the current US women’s cricket team is a true testament of the grassroots efforts initiated by Hinds, whom was responsible for planting the seeds.  
  
Hinds had his calling, in a society of countless variables and endless sporting opportunities, selective moral standards did not reside in his DNA.  As if the gods smiled on him, he was contacted by Cricket For Change, UK to start a cricket program for the visually impaired and physically handicapped, he immediately sprung into action.  No effort was put forward in futility; it was always a duty inscribed on his soul to pave the way for a better tomorrow.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Clifford Hinds on left at a Metropolitan Cricket League final,  right, speaking at a USACA special general meeting at JFK Marriott in New York. Photos by Sham Ali  
**  
Hinds was an intelligent and crafty administrator.  He was able to navigate through a cricket environment that was both turbulent and toxic at times, however Hinds remained steadfast in his approach with a primary focus on bringing all stakeholders together for the betterment of the sport.  Despite his academic accolades, an alumnus of Fordham Law School and an Officer of the Court, he never paraded his accomplishments or pursued the quest for self-aggrandizement; a trait that escaped many in this environment.  Even though his opportunities were endless in a corporate world, he never paraded his accomplishments, instead Hinds chose his brethren of all ages and walked calmly amongst them with that rare air of humility.  He was ever so willing to offer invaluable counsel to the youths pushing them to understand that their possibilities were limitless.  
  
As a loyal student of the game, if for some reason one so chose to engage Hinds at a cricket match, they had to be prepared for his many stories underscoring his point, notwithstanding a few trappings minced into the conversation, perhaps for the entire duration of the cricket match.  His judgments were based not merely on the wholesome understanding of the game but on a wider understanding of society, history and human behavior, and his ability to connect the dots.  Like all good administrators, he was observant and deeply affected by the failings of the leagues and clubs.  In his later years, he remained aggrieved by the gradual decline of leadership standards at the turn of the century, and a new generation’s contempt for tested methods and a nonchalant disregard for the spirit of the game, but more so, in the last decade and a half by the moral turpitude and dismissiveness by corporate forces that acted with impunity and trampled upon cricket in the NY region that deemed it insignificant.  
  
His idiosyncrasies often collided, even as he grappled with his own complexities which appeared at greater than the sum of its parts.  He was fearless and frank, sometimes too frank, he was bold sometimes too much so, and at times quite sensitive for a person who never held back from expressing his views on the affairs of the game.   
  
Hinds led the MCL with distinction and an undying love for cricket.  He proudly stood on the shoulders of past leaders of the MCL and was immediately preceded as President by the likes of Derrick Scott and Clement ‘Busta‘ Lawrence.  He in turn provided an equal platform for those who succeeded him, namely Mascelles Bailey, Sam Belnavis, Trevor Walfall, Clifford Roye and presently Dervon Wallace.  His earnest hope for the game in all of his endeavors was to ignite the passion and fuel the fire that resides in all cricketers.  Unfortunately, that passion was dimmed and transformed into razzmatazz entertainment at the turn of the century, and the game that once prided itself on the highest standards of quality, class and finesse became poorer for it.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Hinds at a New York Region marketing meeting.**  
  
He was an unapologetic romantic, showering those he spoke about with praise and devotion and, more-often-than-not, in a rush of compound adjectives.  In his exchanges, sentimentality or nostalgia were qualities to cherish.  Hinds retained an almost boy-like enthusiasm for cricket into his adult years and a completely non-envious admiration for its performers; his is the blend of romanticism, relish and sheer delight.  A gentleman of not mere surface charm or the easy lightness of confident sociability, he made sure he fulfilled his duties and obligations without drawing attention to himself or making a fuss.  The players will miss a friend and officials will be saddened by the absence of a colleague -- few were prepared for the end.  That confident gentleman with another plan in a folder rolled in hand, his signature wide brimmed cricket hat, in his chair at the cricket ground, holding court, but never missing a ball, will no longer be there.  
  
Clifford Hinds was a class act!  Above all he was always courteous, constant, and always the same, whatever the circumstances or the company as he was always – warm, self-deprecating, and concerned about the lives of others and his willingness to offer help and advice were central to his life and his values; the qualities of a caring man.  
  
For a confident, aggressive man who could have written an exhaustive book on the artless art of leadership on and off the cricket field, he was a better and more caring person while retaining his sense of humor.  His oration could be too florid for some tastes as he was a loveable old rogue when it came to embellishments - it was often joked that in his trips down memory lane Hinds had often inadvertently imagined himself, after a few trips to the bar, as he dipped into his imaginary shelves of cricket tours, he had an eye for greater truths.  You could tell from just one ball bowled or one shot played that he was a cricketer of good ilk.  His hard work was driven by the desire to give a full expression of himself, and he did it not with a bat or ball but dignified with a leader’s pen which gave the game that signature symbolism of a purposeful practitioner.  
  
Hinds was a man of substance, morally serious and intellectually curious.  For all his understatement, he couldn't fail to convey those qualities to anyone who watched him properly.  He loved life but life does not allow us to design our departures, and Hinds got another lease on life after a dreaded diagnosis years ago, and thereafter, his battles with illness lent his features an eerie plasticity.  His face, which once had a craggy grandeur, began to show signs of fragility, and that echo in his voice had lost a few decibels, yet it didn't slow down -- quite visibly, an illustrious journey was nearing the end.  He was tired and frail and lost a major percent of his body mass, however, that ‘heart’ of his and his unwavering passion for the game never relented, it just picked him up and got him to the cricket ground for ‘more talk’ and ‘nuff talk.’  His physical structure was bordering on skeletal, a material contrast versus the sturdy, gregarious character he had been for most of his eventful life.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Photo by Sham Ali**  
  
When the cricket world deliberates the who’s who amongst those that have made a difference to the game during their lifetime, the name Clifford S. Hinds will ring loudly in the minds of cricketers and administrators in the United States and undoubtedly will be engraved in the historic annals of US Cricket.  
  
The most glowing accolades that may be bestowed upon a Cricket legend are usually attributable to his on-the-field performance at the national and international level.  Such recognition, though not misplaced, is at times incomplete as not nearly enough attention and recognition is directed to the grassroots cricketers and administrators.  Throughout the rich legacy that is West Indian Cricket, few have consistently delivered at the extraordinary level deserving of vigorous and complete recognition for performance away from the national limelight.  Clifford Hinds is a monumental exception because of his enduring, determined, persistent and successful work as a cricket administrator in the United States.  Befittingly, in 2009, cricket’s most prestigious organization – the International Cricket Council (ICC)– bestowed upon Clifford S. Hinds the coveted International Cricket Council Centenary Medal of Honor for his stellar and untiring contributions to cricket.  It was only a matter of time that another prestigious cricket fraternity - the United States Cricket Hall of Fame in Hartford, Connecticut, also honored the pioneering work of Clifford S. Hinds in 2010.  Who knew what else was behind the vision of this dedicated student of the game towering with all the past inductees.  The entire cricket family saluted him for his unprecedented contribution to cricket, and when asked about his International Cricket Council (ICC) Centenary Medal of Honor award, he stated rather humbly with a little twinkle in his eyes, “I made my contribution for the mere love of the game.”  
  
It was with that love, where many cricketers flatter to deceive, Clifford S. Hinds’ runs deep.  He was the 'link' man binding players to officials in a manner to be envied, and he was at the helm when the MCL was the premier league in the New York cricket world.  Pride and differences in opinions have caused plenty of arguments and disagreements and lost friendships.  Hinds was never carried away with the success and requisite need for the development of cricket; hence, he often found a way to bridge men and their might under one cloud.  
  
After serving his term as President of the MCL, Hinds remained active.  There is little doubt that Clifford Hinds was one of the MCL’s true loyalists; man of many parts, a pioneer, a steadfast character, a cricketer and an official of rare gifts.  There is something mystical about his work, as if an attempt was made to draw a line under all that had gone before, but that another force remained to deny it.  We shall never know, but behind that affable manner hid inner steel, removed his mask and put a creative mind to rest.  By being so spiritually aware of what was beyond the physical world, he became an irresistible conscience for those of us left behind.  The game ignores his teachings, and leaders their duty at their own peril. Hinds would often connect with me on my articles on cricket, the controversial ones, and sang praises especially of those on the obituaries of the MCL stalwarts in his true self “Sam boi, you writing. I thought you well” to which I would respond, “wait until I write yours, Cats”.  
  
I will miss him.  We will miss him.  The wisdom, the kindness, the profound incisions, the child-like simplicity of his humor, the colloquial realism, the lack of ego, the debatable rants, and how this and that collide, the high standards, the hard but fair marking, the counsel given and taken, disdain of invectives, the shared love of so many things that stretch heart and mind.  Above them all is friendship.  His vision ensured that his fame was less dimmed in old age than that of his peers, some of whom without such a focus, faded from memory.  Clifford Hinds is survived by his loving children and grandchildren.   
  
That once full-of-life rambunctious character that once bore its fame slowly, surrendered a frail and fragile frame on its journey to dwell on a land that is fairer than day.  Clifford S. Hinds is gone! Laid to rest. Farewell to a Pioneer. Farewell to a Giant. Salute to a Dear Friend.

articles.content:
**DAVIS, Calif., Sept. 29, 2026** — The East Bay Blazers closed their four-game short season with six players from Blazers Cricket Academy making their senior-team debuts through the club's Elite Pathway program.  
  
The sixth and final debut came from Aadhav Iyer, who played in the Blazers' fourth game against the San Ramon Grizzlies on Sept. 26 at Davis Cricket Ground.  
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/2fa411894121_1790692651.jpg)

**Aadhav Iyer is one of six Blazers Cricket Academy players to make their Minor League Cricket debuts in the 2026 season.**  
  
The shortened season followed a deliberate decision by Blazers management. After qualifying for the playoffs and winning their division in each of the previous three seasons, the club opted not to pursue this year's playoff campaign. Instead, the Blazers focused on player development and creating opportunities for academy students to transition into senior-level competition.  
  
A Pathway From Academy to Match Day  
The Elite Pathway program is designed to bridge the gap between academy development and senior competition. Six academy players were given an opportunity to gain experience at the senior level during the season, providing a direct route from the club's youth development program to competitive match play.  
  
"Winning three straight division titles has been a proud achievement for everyone at the Blazers, but a club is only as strong as the players coming through behind it," said Biju Nair of the East Bay Blazers. "This season was about giving our academy students a real opportunity, and seeing six of them debut, including Aadhav in our final game, tells us we made the right call. We're building for the long term."  
  
**Season Highlights**  
• The Blazers completed a four-game short season.  
• Six Blazers Cricket Academy players made their senior-team debuts through the Elite Pathway program.  
• Aadhav Iyer made his debut in Game 4 against the San Ramon Grizzlies on Sept. 26 at Davis Cricket Ground.  
• The Blazers had qualified for the playoffs and won their division in each of the previous three seasons.

articles.title: Remembering Mr. Clifford S. Hinds — A Life Dedicated To Cricket
articles.excerpt: Clifford S. Hinds devoted decades to developing cricket in New York and the Tri-State area, with a particular commitment to youth development and creating opportunities for future
articles.content:
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/ce0963222a3f_1790515981.jpg)

**Clifford S. Hinds devoted decades to developing cricket in New York and the Tri-State area, with a particular commitment to youth development and creating opportunities for future generations of American cricketers.**  
  
**Sept. 25, 1942 – Sept. 21, 2026**  
The passing of Mr. Clifford S. Hinds is a tremendous loss to the cricket fraternity of New York, the Tri-State area, and the wider American cricket community.  
  
Mr. Hinds was among those remarkable individuals who devoted a significant part of their lives to establishing, strengthening, and expanding cricket in a region where the sport needed committed people willing to invest their personal time and energy to help it grow.  
  
For decades, New York cricket benefited from his presence, involvement, and tireless efforts. He served the game in numerous capacities, but his greatest contribution may be found in the generations of young cricketers whose journeys were made possible through the programs and opportunities he helped create.  
  
Youth cricket was especially close to his heart. At a time when organized pathways for young cricketers in the United States were limited, Mr. Hinds dedicated countless hours to developing an environment where youngsters could practice, compete, learn the values of the game, and progress to higher levels of cricket.  
  
Through his involvement with New York Tri-State youth cricket, he helped bring together young players, coaches, administrators, parents, clubs, and communities around a common purpose: to give the next generation an opportunity to play and advance in cricket.  
  
The true value of that contribution cannot simply be measured by the number of matches played or tournaments organized. It can be seen in the young cricketers who developed through these programs, in those who went on to represent the United States at youth and senior levels, and in the many families who became part of the growing cricket community across New York and the Tri-State region.  
  
Mr. Hinds understood something very important: the future of cricket depends upon what we invest in our youth today.  
  
He gave one of life's most precious gifts to that mission — his time.  
  
Year after year, he continued giving his time to young players and to the development of cricket. Much of this work happened away from public recognition: organizing, mentoring, guiding, creating opportunities, supporting programs, and helping young cricketers find a pathway forward.  
  
His efforts also extended to advancing opportunities for women and girls in cricket, helping to broaden participation and strengthen the sport's foundation in the United States.  
  
For those of us associated with cricket in New York, Mr. Hinds represents an important chapter in our cricket history. The community we see today was built through the dedication of individuals like him who believed in the game long before cricket had the visibility and opportunities it enjoys today.  
  
His physical presence may no longer be with us, but his contribution lives on every time a young player walks onto a cricket field in New York with the dream of representing the United States.  
That is a legacy no scoreboard can measure.  
  
My thoughts and prayers are with the Hinds family, his friends, fellow administrators, former players, and everyone across the cricket community who had the privilege of knowing him.  
  
Thank you, Mr. Clifford S. Hinds, for giving so many valuable years of your life to cricket, to New York, to the Tri-State cricket community, and, most importantly, to our youth.  
  
The seeds you planted will continue to grow through future generations of American cricketers.  
  
May your soul rest in eternal peace. Om Shanti.  
  
**With heartfelt remembrance and the highest regard,  
Rahul Sharma**

articles.excerpt: Advaith Dhumal Rao(left) and Rayyan Ketekar made their Minor League Cricket debuts for the East Bay Blazers, with Ketekar taking 1 for 5 against Silicon Valley Strikers. Calif. — S
articles.content:
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/329ec65611d5_1790514737.jpg)

**Advaith Dhumal Rao(left) and Rayyan Ketekar made their Minor League Cricket debuts for the East Bay Blazers, with Ketekar taking 1 for 5 against Silicon Valley Strikers.  
  
Calif. — Sept. 26, 2026** — Two more graduates of the Blazers Cricket Academy Elite Pathway Program made their Minor League Cricket (MiLC) debuts for the East Bay Blazers on Sept. 25, as the team faced the Silicon Valley Strikers in a West Division match.  
  
Rayyan Ketekar made an immediate impact with the ball, taking 1 for 5 from two overs. He bowled seven dot balls and finished with an economy rate of 2.50, the best among the Blazers bowlers in the match.  
  
Advaith Dhumal Rao also made his MiLC debut in the same fixture, marking another step in his progression from the Academy pathway to senior-level cricket.  
  
The debuts continue the progression of players from the Blazers Cricket Academy Elite Pathway Program into Minor League Cricket. The program provides young cricketers in the Bay Area with a structured route from academy training to competitive cricket at the domestic level in the United States.  
  
“This year marks a stepping stone for the Academy as we move in a direction where the focus is on youth — building our homegrown players and developing them for the bigger platform,” said Biju Nair, Founder and CEO of Blazers Cricket Academy.  
  
“We’re excited to be part of the journey at Blazers Cricket Academy and grateful for the opportunity to play at the Minor League level,” Ketekar and Dhumal Rao said in a joint statement.  
  
The East Bay Blazers are scheduled to play their fourth game of the season on Saturday, September 26, against the San Ramon Grizzlies.  
  
**About Blazers Cricket Academy**  
Founded in 2023 in the Bay Area, Blazers Cricket Academy has trained more than 500 players. The Academy develops young cricketers through structured coaching and its Elite Pathway Program, which prepares players for competitive and Minor League cricket.

articles.title: Acc Announces U.s. School Cricket Pathway With Scholarships And High-performance Training
articles.excerpt: The American Cricket Council (ACC) has announced a nationwide school and collegiate cricket initiative aimed at creating structured pathways for young players, high-performance tra
articles.content:
The American Cricket Council (ACC) has announced a nationwide school and collegiate cricket initiative aimed at creating structured pathways for young players, high-performance training and scholarship opportunities across the United States.  
  
The initiative was announced in North Brunswick, New Jersey, and is designed around a model similar to the National Federation of State High School Associations (NFHS) and the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), with the goal of establishing a more organized framework for cricket within the American school and college sports system.  
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/f2fa4f1a18ec_1790339809.jpg)

**Former West Indies captain Shivnarine Chanderpaul will lead the American Cricket Council’s high-performance coaching program as part of its new national school and collegiate cricket initiative. Photo courtesy of Carl Fourie/Gallo Images**  
  
Former West Indies captain, batter and Cricket Hall of Famer Shivnarine Chanderpaul will lead the high-performance coaching program, including a Center for Excellence for players and a dedicated coach training center.  
  
Chanderpaul, who previously served as head coach of the USA women's national team and led Jamaica Tallawahs to a Caribbean Premier League (CPL) championship, will work alongside multisport coach Jatin Patel and a team of professional coaches from across North America.  
  
The program will include high-performance training and a virtual academy focused on mentorship and technical development for grassroots players. Orlando, Florida, will serve as the ACC's second home for high-performance training camps supporting planned inter-school and college Super Cup events and leagues.  
  
The initiative is being developed through a partnership involving the ACC, Cricket Hall of Fame, TV Asia and ACEC, with the program expected to provide opportunities for schools, colleges, academies and individual student-athletes.  
  
"Our goal is to integrate cricket directly into the fabric of American high school and college sports culture," said Jatin Patel, Chair. "By combining high-performance coaching, standardized educational curricula, and clear scholarship pathways, we are providing young athletes with a legitimate career and academic future in sport Cricket."  
  
National registration for schools, colleges, academies and individual student-athletes is scheduled to open on October 2, 2026. The ACC said detailed program guidelines, tournament structures and scholarship criteria will be unveiled following the official launch event.  
  
The initiative represents another effort to establish more formal development routes for young cricketers in the United States, with registration, high-performance training, competitions and scholarship opportunities forming the initial framework. Further details on the structure and eligibility requirements are expected after the October launch.

articles.title: Kingsmen Xi Launches New Jersey Campaign In Mcl Fall T20 Premier
articles.excerpt: Kingsmen XI opened its Millennium Cricket League (MCL) Fall T20 Premier Division campaign in New Jersey with a heavy defeat to TeknuQi Warriors before responding with a much-improv
articles.content:
Kingsmen XI opened its Millennium Cricket League (MCL) Fall T20 Premier Division campaign in New Jersey with a heavy defeat to TeknuQi Warriors before responding with a much-improved bowling performance against DreamCricket Sparks Warriors in its second match.  
  
The New York-based club has expanded into New Jersey for the Fall T20 Premier Division, with founder Daryl Heerasingh saying the move is intended to provide greater opportunities for the club’s young players to compete alongside Major League Cricket and Minor League Cricket players from across the Tri-State area.  
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/9058f478c090_1790259746.jpg)

**Sixteen-year-old Ethan Silas made an assured Kingsmen XI debut, scoring 44 to anchor the chase against DreamCricket Sparks Warriors in the MCL Fall T20 Premier Division.**  
  
Kingsmen’s first Premier Division match against TeknuQi Warriors proved a difficult introduction. Sent in to bat, Kingsmen were restricted to 97 for 9, with Kevin Christian top-scoring with 25 and Anthony Providence contributing 22.  
  
Preet Shah was the standout bowler for Kingsmen, taking 3 for 12 from his four overs. Miraaj Naidu and Muhammad Ali claimed two wickets apiece, but Kingsmen were unable to build a sufficiently competitive total.  
  
TeknuQi made quick work of the chase, driven by an outstanding innings from Syed Abdullah. He struck 83 from just 37 balls, hitting four fours and 10 sixes, to take the Warriors comfortably through the pursuit.  
  
Vishal Roopnarine was Kingsmen’s only wicket-taker, finishing with 1 for 12 from two overs.  
  
Kingsmen showed a different side in their second game, against DreamCricket Sparks Warriors, producing a disciplined bowling effort to restrict their opponents to 119 in 20 overs.  
  
Antanio Rooplall led the attack with 3 for 19 from four overs, while Darrius Andrews returned 2 for 18 from his four-over spell. The pair helped Kingsmen keep DreamCricket from building a larger total and gave their side a realistic opportunity in the chase.  
  
The response was led by 16-year-old Ethan Silas, who made his Kingsmen XI debut and scored 44. His contribution kept the chase on course during a tense passage of play.  
  
Kevin Augustine added 17 from 11 balls before skipper Heerasingh came to the crease in the 17th over with Kingsmen at 103 for 6. With the match entering its decisive stages, the captain remained composed and scored 14 from eight balls alongside Andrews.  
  
The performances highlighted the contrasting fortunes of Kingsmen’s opening matches. After their batting was exposed against TeknuQi, the team produced a more competitive all-round display against DreamCricket, particularly with the ball and through contributions from its younger players.  
  
The Fall T20 Premier Division campaign gives Kingsmen XI an opportunity to measure its squad against established competition in the Tri-State area. The results of the opening matches will form part of the club’s early push as it continues its first campaign in the New Jersey-based competition.

articles.excerpt: Three graduates of the East Bay Blazers Cricket Academy’s Elite Development Program — Ayaan Khan, Syon Kurdekar and Avyukth Raghunarayan — combined for a late rally against the San
articles.content:
Three graduates of the East Bay Blazers Cricket Academy’s Elite Development Program — Ayaan Khan, Syon Kurdekar and Avyukth Raghunarayan — combined for a late rally against the San Ramon Grizzlies on Sept. 20, 2026, as the Blazers fell 10 runs short in a closely contested chase.  
  
The Blazers, led by Sanjay Krishnamurthi, a top-order batter for the San Francisco Unicorns and a member of the USA national team, featured a lineup that included fellow Unicorns player Saideep Ganesh and Abhishek Paradkar of the Washington Freedom. Krishnamurthi had also recently competed in the ETPL.  
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/f941e5b7d5f0_1789996335.jpg)

**East Bay Blazers Academy graduates Avyukth Raghunarayan, Ayaan Khan and Syon Kurdekar partaking in Minor League Cricket, combined for a late rally against the San Ramon Grizzlies on Sept. 20, 2026.**  
  
The lineup brought together professional players, Academy coaches and emerging youth cricketers, providing the Elite Program graduates with an opportunity to compete alongside experienced players.  
  
Chasing 147 for victory, East Bay Blazers lost wickets through the middle overs and appeared to be falling out of contention. However, the Academy trio combined for 34 runs in the final 2.3 overs, giving the chase a late surge.  
  
Raghunarayan led the scoring during the closing burst with 17 off 10 balls, while Khan contributed a quickfire six off five deliveries. Kurdekar remained unbeaten on 11 off seven balls as the Blazers continued to press until the end.  
  
The effort was not enough to secure victory. East Bay Blazers were dismissed for 136 in 19.4 overs, finishing 10 runs short of the Grizzlies’ 146-8.  
  
Raghunarayan also made an impact with the ball, returning figures of 2-15 from four overs at an economy rate of 3.75. His spell was the most economical of the innings, highlighting his contribution in both departments.  
  
Academy coaches Angelo Perera, Suliman Arabzai, Sidhant Reddy and Faisal Khan Ahmadzai also featured in the Blazers’ playing XI, taking the field alongside players they help develop.  
  
The match brought together established professionals, a USA international, coaching staff and Academy graduates in the same lineup, reflecting the club’s approach to providing young cricketers with opportunities to gain experience in senior-level competition.  
  
Although the Blazers fell short, the Academy viewed the performance as an encouraging sign of its ongoing investment in youth development. The late rally offered its young players an opportunity to demonstrate their composure and skills in a competitive match against experienced opposition.  
  
The Elite Development Program is scheduled to feature in the Blazers’ next two fixtures, with additional emerging players expected to take part. The Academy also announced that its broader development squad would begin featuring on Friday as part of its continued efforts to expand youth cricket in the region.

articles.title: Etpl: Andries Gous’ 90 Leads Edinburgh Castle Rockers To Championship Win
articles.excerpt: Scorecard Edinburgh Castle Rockers chased down Belfast Wolves’ 150 for five with eight balls remaining to secure a seven-wicket victory in the European T20 Premier League final at
articles.content:
**[Scorecard](https://www.etplofficial.com/matches/6a688c61b30844b0969df8c2)**  
Edinburgh Castle Rockers chased down Belfast Wolves’ 150 for five with eight balls remaining to secure a seven-wicket victory in the European T20 Premier League final at Malahide Cricket Ground on Sunday, September 20. Andries Gous anchored the chase with an unbeaten 90 from 61 balls, guiding Edinburgh to 151 for three in 18.4 overs.  
  
After winning the toss and choosing to bowl, Edinburgh restricted Belfast to 150 for five from their 20 overs. Tom Tector top-scored for Belfast with 84 from 62 balls, striking nine fours and two sixes at a strike rate of 135.48.  
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/50844c1fd958_1789925772.jpg)

**Andries Gous scored an unbeaten 90 from 61 balls as Edinburgh Castle Rockers chased 151 to beat Belfast Wolves by seven wickets in the European T20 Premier League final. File photo by Shiek Mohamed**  
  
Belfast made a slow start after Paul Stirling was dismissed for eight in the third over, caught by Jarvis off Trent Boult. Tector and Devon Conway then rebuilt the innings with a 63-run partnership from 51 balls. Conway made 29 from 24 deliveries, including two fours and a six, before he was caught by Delany off Jon Smuts.  
  
Tector continued to hold the innings together through the middle overs, adding 14 with Glenn Maxwell and 10 with Lorcan Tucker. Maxwell made three before falling to Mark Watt, while Tucker was dismissed for six, caught by Smuts off Boult.  
  
Tector's 84 ended with the final ball of the innings when he was bowled by Tom Curran. Harry Manenti remained unbeaten on 16 from 14 balls, including a four, and shared a 45-run fifth-wicket partnership with Tector from 32 deliveries.  
  
Boult was Edinburgh's leading bowler, finishing with two for 21 from four overs, including 13 dot balls. Curran and Watt took one wicket each, while Smuts also claimed a wicket.  
  
Edinburgh's chase began aggressively, with Graham Adair scoring 23 from 14 balls with two fours and two sixes. His dismissal brought Gous to the crease, and he steadily took control of the pursuit.  
  
Gous added 53 for the second wicket with Smuts, who made 15 from 23 balls before being bowled by Matthew Humphreys. Gous then combined with Brandon McMullen for the decisive partnership of the chase, putting on 60 from 46 balls.  
  
McMullen struck three fours in his 17 from 12 balls before he was caught and bowled by Graham Hoey in the 18th over. By then, Edinburgh required only 12 runs from 14 deliveries.  
  
Gous completed the chase alongside Mitchell Santner, who finished unbeaten on two from two balls. Gous's 90 came from 61 deliveries and included eight fours and four sixes, giving him a strike rate of 147.54.  
  
Humphreys and Hoey claimed one wicket apiece for Belfast, while Michael Adair also took a wicket. Edinburgh's chase never lost control after Gous settled in, and the target was reached with 1.2 overs remaining.  
  
The seven-wicket victory sees Edinburgh Castle Rockers finish the European T20 Premier League final on top, while Belfast Wolves' 150 for five was not enough to defend the total despite Tector's substantial contribution.

articles.content:
**[Scorecard](https://www.minorleaguecricket.com/MiLC/results/DBm_1Xm0fPpXIXL1fVzTrg?asfd=Silicon+Valley+Strikers+vs+San+Ramon+Grizzlies&tab=full_scorecard)**  
San Ramon Grizzlies defeated Silicon Valley Strikers by six wickets, chasing down a target of 131 with eight balls to spare in their Minor League Cricket West match in Davis on Saturday Sept. 19th. Captain Shivam Mishra led the chase with 71 off 44 balls after Adnesh Tondale's five-wicket haul had restricted the Strikers to 130-8.  
  
Mishra was named Player of the Match for his match-winning contribution with the bat, having also claimed two wickets in the first innings.  
![](https://usacricketers.com/uploads/5527b8e91ed9_1789917925.jpg)

**Shivam Mishra (right) scored 71 off 44 balls to lead San Ramon Grizzlies past Silicon Valley Strikers by six wickets after Adnesh Tondale (left) claimed five wickets in Minor League Cricket West.**  
  
After winning the toss and electing to bowl, the Grizzlies made early inroads into the Strikers' batting lineup. Tondale dismissed Amogh Arepally for nine and Kamran Hotak for 17, leaving the Strikers at 33-2 in 5.1 overs.  
  
Shehan Jayasuriya provided a counterattack, scoring 30 off 17 balls, including three fours and two sixes. However, Mishra ended his innings at 69-4 in 11.2 overs, with Jayasuriya bowled after striking at 176.47.  
  
Vivaan Jagtiani attempted to rebuild the innings, contributing 28 from 31 deliveries, while Aarnav Iyer added 11. Their efforts helped the Strikers reach 97-5 before Jagtiani fell to Ayan Desai in the 16th over.  
  
Tondale continued to trouble the lower order, dismissing Iyer, captain Gary Graham and Kristopher Ramsaran to finish with 5-19 from four overs, including one maiden. Mishra returned figures of 2-21, while Desai claimed 1-28. The Strikers finished on 130-8, with Naman Patil and Carmi Le Roux unbeaten on two each.  
  
The Grizzlies' chase began with a brief collapse. Carmi Le Roux dismissed Rahul Jariwala for six, while Hotak removed Zahid Zakhil and Sahil Garg in quick succession. At 11-3 after 2.2 overs, the home side faced an early challenge.  
  
Mishra and Manav Nayak then steadied the innings with a decisive partnership. Mishra attacked the bowling, hitting seven fours and four sixes in his 71, while Nayak provided support with a measured unbeaten 42 from 50 balls, including two fours and a six.  
  
The pair took the Grizzlies to 121 before Mishra was caught by wicketkeeper Arepally off Yousuf Zazai in the 18th over. With nine runs required, Nayak remained at the crease alongside Harish Kakani, who finished unbeaten on two.  
  
Nayak and Kakani completed the chase at 134-4 in 18.4 overs, securing the Grizzlies a six-wicket victory.  
  
The result gives San Ramon Grizzlies a win in the Minor League Cricket West competition, while Silicon Valley Strikers will look to recover from a batting performance that was undermined by Tondale's five-wicket haul and an early collapse during the chase.

**Unmukt Chand’s unbeaten 100 and Andre Fletcher’s 72 powered Lone Star Athletics to 219-1 against All Stars in Minor League Cricket Central.**  
  
Chand finished on 100 not out from 67 balls, striking 11 fours and five sixes at a strike rate of 149.25. Fletcher provided the early momentum with 72 from 43 deliveries, including seven fours and four sixes, before being caught off Yuvan Kiran at 163-1 in the 17th over.  
  
The opening partnership between Fletcher and Chand laid the foundation for the imposing total, taking Lone Star Athletics to 163 before the first wicket fell at 16.2 overs. Chand continued to bat through the innings, while captain Kumar accelerated late, scoring 26 not out from just 11 balls, with three sixes at a strike rate of 236.36.

Aarin Nadkarni claimed 1-24, while Andre Fletcher contributed with the ball, taking 1-26. Naqash Basharat made an early impact with 2-9 in two overs, dismissing Gowda and Dar.  
  
All Stars slipped to 56-5 before Siddantham and Dhana Krishna Vardhan Vundavalli attempted to rebuild. Vundavalli scored 16 from 13 balls, but his dismissal at 119-8 in the 19th over left the lower order with too much to do. All Stars closed on 125-9, with Yuvan Kiran unbeaten on five and Shaah on one.  
  
The result gives Lone Star Athletics a commanding win in the Minor League Cricket Central competition, while All Stars will need to address their early batting collapses and inability to contain a powerful top order.

**Nikhil Mudaliar and Saharsh Shwethan scored unbeaten half-centuries to guide Morrisville Raptors to a nine-wicket victory over Atlanta Lightning.**  
  
Atlanta, batting first after Morrisville won the toss and elected to bowl, struggled to build sustained partnerships against a disciplined bowling attack.  
  
Chandrapaul Hemraj top-scored with 27 off 25 balls, hitting three fours, while wicketkeeper Abdulahad Malek contributed 21 from 21 deliveries. Kashyap Prajapati added 16 off 21 balls, but Atlanta lost wickets at regular intervals and were unable to accelerate consistently.

Narisetty was Atlanta’s only successful bowler, taking 1-24 from two overs. The remaining bowlers were unable to break the partnership as Morrisville reached the target in 14.3 overs.  
  
The result gives Morrisville a nine-wicket victory in the Minor League Cricket South competition, while Atlanta will look to address their batting difficulties in their remaining matches. articles.content:

**Eight Blazers Cricket Academy U19 Elite Cohort players have been selected for the Bay Blazers’ 2026 Minor League Cricket squad.**  
  
Eight players from Blazers Cricket Academy’s U19 Elite Cohort have been selected for the Bay Blazers’ Minor League Cricket squad, joining a group led by Sanjay Krishnamurthy and Angelo Perera ahead of the 2026 season, which begins September 18.  
  
The selections provide the academy’s young players with an opportunity to compete alongside established domestic and international cricketers in the Bay Blazers setup.  
  
The eight players making their debut when the new season begins are Aadhav Iyer, Advaith Dhumal Rao, Aryan Mathur, Avyukth Raghunarayan, Ayaan Khan, Rayyan Ketekar, Saaket Bapu and Syon Kurdekar.  
  
The Bay Blazers are the reigning three-time consecutive West Division champions. Krishnamurthy, a member of the San Francisco Unicorns in Major League Cricket (MLC), will captain the side, with Sri Lankan international Perera serving as vice-captain.  
  
The academy’s selections will train and compete alongside senior players, including Saideep Ganesh, Abhishek Paradkar and Faisal Khan. The wider group of players connected to Major League Cricket also includes Nawaz Khan, Hizbullah Durani and Suliman Arabazai.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

For the eight teenagers, the upcoming campaign marks a step into senior-level competition, where they will have the opportunity to gain experience alongside players with professional and international backgrounds.  
  
Blazers Cricket Academy founder and chief executive Biju Nair said the selections reflected the academy’s efforts to establish a structured development route from grassroots cricket to higher levels of the game.  
  
“This is exactly the kind of pathway we set out to build — one that starts at a young age and gives players a real, structured route to the top of the game,” Nair said.  
  
“Seeing eight of our U19 Elite Cohort players step onto the field with Major League Cricket professionals is proof that the work we do at the grassroots level translates directly to opportunity at the highest stage.”  
  
Nair also pointed to the academy’s results in USA Cricket’s pathway programs, including its U15 Bay Area Hub Championship victory in 2026.  
  
The academy’s younger age-group teams have also recorded results in regional competition. Its U13 squad finished runner-up in the Bay Area Hub and reached the final in three consecutive years, according to the academy.  
  
The eight selections add to the academy’s representation in the Bay Area cricket structure and give the players an opportunity to develop through exposure to senior competition.  
  
The Bay Blazers will begin their 2026 Minor League Cricket campaign on September 18, with the eight academy players set to make their debuts as they join the three-time West Division champions.

articles.content:
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Southern Strikers won their third consecutive Elite Division championship after defeating NJ Dream in the final of the 2026 Bay Area Women’s Open.**  
  
The Southern Strikers secured a third consecutive Elite Division title while the Valkyries won the inaugural Premier Division championship as the Bay Area Women's Open concluded on Monday, September 7, in the Bay Area.  
  
The third edition of the tournament featured nine teams and 22 matches over three days, with the introduction of the Premier Division expanding the competition beyond its established Elite Division.  
  
The tournament was jointly organized by three Minor League Cricket teams — the Blazers, Strikers and Grizzlies — with matches played on turf wickets.  
  
**Southern Strikers Make It Three in a Row**  
The Southern Strikers maintained their dominance in the Elite Division, winning the title for the third straight year after chasing down NJ Dream's 149 for 3 in the final at Taarika.  
  
NJ Dream's total was built around an unbeaten 110 from 64 balls by Nikki Doshi, who struck 17 fours and two sixes at a strike rate of 171.88.  
  
The Strikers reached 151 for 5 in 18 overs to win by five wickets with two overs remaining. Aaradhya Vashisth led the chase with an unbeaten 74 from 43 balls, hitting 11 fours and two sixes at a strike rate of 172.09. She was named Player of the Match.  
  
Wicketkeeper Camy Desai contributed 25 from 22 balls, while captain Geetika Kodali finished unbeaten on 9.  
  
Doshi was named both Best Batter and Most Valuable Player after scoring 217 runs at a strike rate of 144.67. More than half of those runs came in her unbeaten century in the final.  
  
Simiksha Sivakumar claimed the Best Bowler award after taking seven wickets at an average of 12.14. Desai was named Best Wicketkeeper with eight dismissals, while Southern Strikers teammate Jessica Willathgamuwa received the Best Fielder award after five catches and a run out.  
  
“To clinch the title for the third year running says a great deal about this group,” said Suresh Vallabhaneni, co-owner of the Southern Strikers. “The Bay Area Open has grown in leaps and bounds in 2026, both in the quality of the cricket and in the infrastructure around it. We are proud to be part of that journey.”  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Valkyries captured the inaugural Premier Division title at the 2026 Bay Area Women’s Open.**  
  
**Valkyries Break Through for a Debut Title**  
The Valkyries claimed the first Premier Division championship after restricting NorCal Panthers to 82 for 6 in the final at Santa Clara.  
  
The Valkyries completed the chase in 18 overs, reaching 85 for 1 to secure a nine-wicket victory. Aadhya Sah was named Player of the Match.  
  
Sah also took the Premier Division's Best Fielder award after recording five catches and a run out.  
  
Ishika Peddyreddy was named Most Valuable Player following an all-round campaign that produced 121 runs, four wickets and a catch. Anannya Kulkarni was the Best Batter with 122 runs at a strike rate of 79.74.  
  
Laya Balakrishnan took the Best Bowler award after claiming 10 wickets at an average of 6.09 and an economy rate of 4.06. Diya Prashanth was named Best Wicketkeeper with 14 dismissals.  
  
“The Bay Area Open is the best platform there is for girls and women to grow in quality cricket,” said Lalith Kancharla, owner of the Valkyries. “2026 was remarkably big and of a very high standard, and we thank the organizers for what they have built.”  
  
**Built and Backed by Three Minor League Teams**  
The collaboration between the Blazers, Strikers and Grizzlies enabled organizers to pool grounds, equipment, match officials and volunteers as the tournament expanded.  
  
The 2026 edition recorded 165 player registrations, the highest total in the tournament's history, while more than 32 players in the field had represented their countries at international level.  
  
“This tournament has grown year over year, with 2026 being the biggest event in the nation for women's cricket,” said Biju Nair, founder and CEO of Blazers Cricket Academy and organizer of the Bay Area Open.  
  
The organizers also added the Premier Division, staged all matches on three turf wickets and provided full video production coverage.  
  
“165 registrations, more than 32 players who have played international cricket, three turf wickets and top-class video production — that is the standard we set ourselves this year. Adding the Premier Division gave every team, whatever stage it is at, something real to play for,” Nair said.  
  
**A National Benchmark for Women's Cricket**  
The two-division structure gave established teams the Elite Division while providing developing sides with another route to a championship, illustrated by the Valkyries' victory in the inaugural Premier Division.  
  
All matches were played on turf wickets and recorded by a full video production crew, providing coverage for players, families and supporters following the tournament remotely.  
  
With the Southern Strikers extending their Elite Division run and the Valkyries becoming the first Premier Division champions, the 2026 Bay Area Women's Open concluded with two different stories: continued dominance at the top and a new championship pathway for emerging teams.

articles.content:
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**John Aaron**  
  
For John Aaron, cricket has never been simply a game. It has been a lifelong vehicle for service, community building, opportunity, and developing young people—particularly women and girls seeking pathways to advance in American cricket.  
  
For more than four decades, Aaron has served the sport at virtually every level in the United States—as a club administrator, league president, regional chairman, national governing-body executive, USA national team manager, championship-winning women's team manager, cricket journalist, Hall of Fame inductee, and advocate for women's and youth cricket.  
  
His journey has taken him from Guyana's cricket culture to club and league administration in New York, national cricket governance, and ultimately the international stage as Team Manager of the United States women's national teams.  
  
Throughout that journey, one principle has remained constant: service to the game and to the people who play it.  
  
**Cricket Heritage**  
Aaron's attachment to cricket began long before he entered administration.  
  
Born in Georgetown, Guyana, he grew up in a family in which the sport was deeply embedded. His father, Reggie Aaron, was associated with the historic Malteenoes Sports Club and was a cricketer, umpire, commentator, and writer. His older brother, Keith Aubrey Aaron, was a Guyana scholar and youth cricketer who captained the Guyana national Under-20 side and led a Guyana Colts XI against a visiting England team in 1968.  
  
Keith encouraged his younger brother to become involved in cricket administration after John settled in the United States. John Aaron also credits Sir Clive Lloyd, Alvin Kallicharran, and Michael Holding, among other West Indies legends, with encouraging him along the way.  
  
That encouragement would help launch more than four decades of service to American cricket.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**A victorious Atlantis women's team at a GWCA T20 tournament**  
  
**Championship Success with the Atlantis Women**  
Aaron's commitment to women's cricket is particularly evident in his management of representative Atlantis Cricket Club–NY women's teams in an annual Georgia Women Cricket Association (GWCA) Women's T20 Tournament, held in Georgia.  
  
As Team Manager, Aaron has guided Atlantis women's teams to an impressive five championship titles in seven attempts at the GWCA annual tournaments. The Atlantis teams included such international players as Stafanie Taylor and Tremayne Smartt.  
  
The Atlantis women's program's significance, however, extends beyond championships.  
  
The representative teams Aaron managed have featured eight women cricketers who have represented USA national teams in International Cricket Council (ICC) tournaments.  
  
That combination of championship success and national-team representation illustrates a key element of Aaron's approach to cricket development: creating competitive environments where talented female cricketers can test and develop their skills while preparing for opportunities at higher levels of the sport.  
  
The Atlantis women's program consequently became an important bridge between two major areas of Aaron's cricket career—his decades-long commitment to Atlantis and his subsequent service with the USA Women's Senior and Under-19 national teams.  
  
Five championships in seven attempts provide an impressive measure of competitive success. The progression of eight Atlantis women to USA squads competing in ICC tournaments provides an equally meaningful measure of development.  
  
For Aaron, both achievements reflect a philosophy that success should be measured not only by trophies won, but also by opportunities created for players to develop, advance, and represent their country.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**An Atlantis Men's Squad in the EACA league**  
  
**Atlantis Cricket Club–NY**  
Aaron's formal involvement in cricket administration began in the mid-1980s with Atlantis Cricket Club–NY, a New York-based cricket organization founded in 1966.  
  
Atlantis became the foundation for much of his philosophy on cricket administration: a cricket club should be more than a collection of players who meet on weekends to play matches. It should also be an institution that contributes meaningfully to the community it represents.  
  
Beginning in 1985–86, Aaron served Atlantis in several capacities, including Secretary, President, and Men's Cricket Manager. Published accounts credit him with about 23 years of service in senior administrative positions early in his Atlantis career.  
  
His club presidency was particularly associated with expanding the club's identity and social responsibilities beyond the boundary.  
  
Under the club's familiar expression, "Atlantis…more than just cricket!", community engagement became an important part of the organization.   
  
Atlantis supported educational scholarships, local charitable initiatives, responses to international human tragedies, Habitat for Humanity, New York City clothing, food, and toy drives, assistance to cricketers and families experiencing hardship, and programs designed to introduce cricket to young people.  
  
To that end, in 2001 Aaron established an annual Atlantis educational scholarship stipend fund following the tragic circumstances surrounding the September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States that claimed the life of a daughter of one of the club's members - Shevonne Mentis. The initiative aimed to respond to tragedies by creating something enduring and positive for young people within the broader Atlantis family and community.  
  
Through the club's 501(c)(3) charitable organization, the scholarship program has since distributed financial stipends to more than 35 students entering college, extending Atlantis' contribution well beyond cricket and providing tangible support to young people pursuing higher education.  
  
The scholarship initiative became one of the clearest expressions of the philosophy Aaron sought to promote within the club: that the value of a cricket organization should be measured not only by its performances and championships on the field, but also by the difference it makes in people's lives away from it.  
  
In 2011, Aaron also helped facilitate an initiative through which Atlantis and the United States Youth Cricket Association introduced cricket to students at Peninsula Preparatory Academy in Rockaway Park, Queens.  
  
Women and girls became an increasingly important part of that philosophy. Aaron supported the development of women's cricket within Atlantis at a time when opportunities for female cricketers in the United States were considerably more limited than they are today.  
  
Decades after first serving the organization, his relationship with Atlantis remains central to his cricket life. With Atlantis Cricket Club-NY celebrating its 60th anniversary this year, Aaron continues to serve as the club's Executive Vice President.  
  
**Championship Success with the Atlantis Women**  
Aaron's commitment to women's cricket is particularly evident in his management of representative Atlantis Cricket Club–NY women's teams.  
  
As Team Manager, Aaron has guided Atlantis women's teams to an impressive five championship titles in seven attempts at the GWCA annual Women's T20 tournament in Georgia. The Atlantis teams included such international players as Stafanie Taylor and Tremayne Smartt.  
  
The Atlantis women's program's significance, however, extends beyond championships.  
  
The representative teams Aaron managed have featured eight women cricketers who have represented USA national teams in International Cricket Council (ICC) tournaments.  
  
That combination of championship success and national-team representation illustrates a key element of Aaron's approach to cricket development: creating competitive environments where talented female cricketers can test and develop their skills while preparing for opportunities at higher levels of the sport.  
  
The Atlantis women's program consequently became an important bridge between two major areas of Aaron's cricket career—his decades-long commitment to Atlantis and his subsequent service with the USA Women's Senior and Under-19 national teams.  
  
Five championships in seven attempts provide an impressive measure of competitive success. The progression of eight Atlantis women to USA squads competing in ICC tournaments provides an equally meaningful measure of development.  
  
For Aaron, both achievements reflect a philosophy that success should be measured not only by trophies won, but also by opportunities created for players to develop, advance, and represent their country.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**John Aaron - During a live radio interview at the BBC studios in Gloucester, UK.**  
  
**From Club Cricket to League Leadership**  
Aaron's administrative involvement expanded beyond Atlantis to the Eastern American Cricket Association (EACA), historically one of New York's prominent cricket leagues.  
  
He served as both Secretary and President of the EACA, bringing many of the principles he developed at Atlantis to league administration.  
  
His service later advanced to the regional level when he became Chairman of the New York Cricket Region and its representative on the national governing body for cricket in the USA, representing seven leagues in the New York metropolitan area.  
  
Those appointments placed Aaron at an important intersection of club, league, regional, and national cricket administration and broadened his involvement in developing and governing cricket throughout the New York metropolitan area.  
  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**John Aaron (At left) with USA Senior Men's Head Coach Pubudu Dassanayake. File photo by Shem Rodney**  
  
**National Cricket Administration**  
Aaron eventually moved into national administration with the United States of America Cricket Association (USACA), then the ICC-recognized national governing body for cricket in the United States.  
  
He was elected USACA Executive Secretary in 2008 and served through 2011.  
  
American cricket governance was particularly challenging during that period. USACA had experienced ICC suspensions and significant internal disagreements.  
  
Aaron became involved in reconciliation and governance efforts during that period. He chaired a League Presidents Reconciliation Commission established following USACA's second ICC suspension and had earlier served on a Constitution Review Committee chaired by former West Indies Cricket Board President Ken Gordon.  
  
In 2009, Aaron represented USACA at the International Cricket Council Annual General Meeting in Dubai, UAE.  
  
After leaving USACA, he helped found the American Cricket Federation and served as its Secretary from 2012 to 2015.  
  
Throughout these administrative assignments, Aaron advocated for improved governance, stronger development structures, and greater opportunities for youth and women within American cricket.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**A victorious USA Senior Women’s Americas Qualifier team with John Aaron (2nd from right) and former USA Women's Head Coach Charlotte Dickinson (2nd from left).**  
  
**An Advocate for Women's Cricket**  
One theme has remained particularly consistent throughout Aaron's administrative career: his advocacy for greater opportunities for female cricketers.  
  
That commitment began well before women's cricket expanded rapidly and gained greater international visibility.  
  
By the early 2010s, Aaron was publicly advocating for stronger representation and development opportunities for women within American cricket administration.  
  
His involvement with the Atlantis women's teams put that commitment into practice. The five GWCA championships and the emergence of eight USA national representatives from Atlantis women's teams showed how sustained investment in competitive opportunities could strengthen the broader national pathway.  
  
Years later, Aaron's advocacy evolved from club and administrative involvement into the direct responsibility of managing America's national women's teams.  
  
**Managing Team USA**  
Beginning in 2021, Aaron entered one of the most significant chapters of his cricket career when he became involved in helping manage the USA women's national program.  
  
Following an exhaustive USA Cricket (USAC) recruitment and interview process, he was appointed national team manager of the USA Women's Senior and Under-19 national teams.  
  
Over the ensuing years, his assignments took him to international competitions, ICC qualifying tournaments, and bilateral series in the United States and abroad.  
  
His Team USA travels included assignments in the United States, Mexico, the Caribbean, the United Arab Emirates, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Argentina, and the Netherlands.  
  
The role placed Aaron alongside generations of American women seeking to establish the United States as an increasingly competitive force in international women's cricket.  
  
It also allowed him to bring decades of administrative experience and his longstanding commitment to women's cricket directly into the national-team environment.  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**John Aaron with the USA women's squad in Malaysia**  
  
**Three Successful ICC Americas Region Campaigns**  
Notable achievements during Aaron's national-team tenure include three successful ICC Americas regional campaigns that advanced the team along the global qualification pathway.  
  
In 2021, Aaron served as Team Manager during the USA women's successful ICC Americas qualifying campaign in Mexico.  
  
In 2023, he again served as Team Manager as the USA women competed successfully in the ICC Women's T20 World Cup Americas Qualifier in California.  
  
The United States women followed up with another successful Americas qualifying campaign, under John Aaron, in Buenos Aires, Argentina, in 2025.  
  
Together, the 2021, 2023, and 2025 campaigns represented an important period of sustained regional success for the USA women's program, with Aaron serving as Team Manager throughout.  
  
**Building the USA Women's Under-19 Program**  
Aaron's work with the USA Women's Under-19 team became another significant part of his national service.  
  
The emerging American players were being prepared not simply for age-group competition, but as the next generation of senior national-team cricketers.  
  
A breakthrough came during the team’s 2022 tour of the United Arab Emirates, with former West Indies batting great Shivnarine Chanderpaul as Head Coach and Aaron as Team Manager. The USA contested a five-match bilateral series against the UAE Women’s Under-19 team at the ICC Academy in Dubai, which advanced to a deciding fifth match.  
  
USA prevailed by 10 runs to win the series 3–2, giving the young American squad an important international success ahead of the inaugural ICC Women’s Under-19 Cricket World Cup.  
  
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,) **Manager John Aaron (2nd from right) and the USA Senior Women’s Team, ICC Americas Champions, and USA Women's National Head Coach Hilton Moreeng (Standing 2nd from left)**  
  
**A Historic World Cup in South Africa**  
The following January brought an even greater milestone. The USA qualified for the inaugural ICC Under-19 Women’s T20 World Cup in South Africa in 2023—the first ICC age-group World Cup for women.  
  
Aaron traveled to South Africa as Team Manager of the United States Women’s Under-19 national team, working alongside Head Coach Shivnarine Chanderpaul and the team’s support staff.  
  
For the young American players, appearing on a global stage alongside the world’s established cricket nations represented a landmark moment.  
  
For Aaron, it marked another stage in a journey that had begun decades earlier in New York club cricket.  
  
The progression was particularly fitting: from creating opportunities for women at Atlantis to helping manage some of America’s most promising young female cricketers on a World Cup stage.  
  
**Caribbean Competition and Bilateral Success**  
Aaron also managed USA women’s teams through a productive series of encounters with Caribbean opposition.  
  
During this period, USA Under-19 women’s teams competed successfully in Trinidad & Tobago, going unbeaten against Jamaica, Barbados, Trinidad & Tobago, Guyana, the Windward Islands, and the Leeward Islands. The USA Under-19 women later defeated the West Indies Under-19 women 4–1 in Florida in a bilateral series.  
  
The teams met again in Trinidad & Tobago in 2025, where the USA Under-19 women recorded another bilateral series victory, defeating the West Indies Under-19 side 3–1.  
  
These contests gave the American players valuable competition against cricketers emerging from one of the world’s most historic cricket regions.  
  
Aaron’s national-team résumé also included matches against the United Arab Emirates and Zimbabwe, including notable USA victories over ICC Full Member Zimbabwe in a T20 and again in an ODI at Grand Prairie Stadium in Dallas, TX.  
  
These tours and bilateral series formed part of a broader effort to give emerging American female cricketers meaningful international competition and the experience needed to advance on the global stage.  
  
In November 2021, the USA Senior Women’s team, coached by former Australian international Julia Price and managed by John Aaron, participated in a COVID-19-interrupted ICC Women’s Cricket World Cup Qualifier in Zimbabwe.  
  
**Cricket Journalist and Chronicler**  
Aaron’s contribution to cricket has never been limited to administration and team management.  
  
For decades, he has also documented the sport as a writer and photographer, particularly within the New York and American cricket communities.  
  
Under the byline John L. Aaron, his work has chronicled matches, players, administrators, organizations, and issues affecting cricket in the United States. That journalism has helped preserve portions of American cricket history that might otherwise have received little attention from mainstream media.  
  
His contributions were recognized in 2001, when he received the Cricket Hall of Fame President’s Award for Outstanding Journalism.  
  
The honor reflected another dimension of his service to the sport: not simply participating in American cricket history, but helping to document it.  
**  
Cricket Hall of Fame**  
Another major personal honor followed in 2012.  
  
Aaron was selected for induction into the Cricket Hall of Fame in recognition of his contributions to cricket administration, journalism, and development of the sport.  
  
His induction reflected a career that had already progressed from Atlantis through the Eastern American Cricket Association, New York Cricket Region, and national cricket administration.  
  
At his induction, however, Aaron characteristically focused less on personal achievement than on those who cultivated his love of cricket—particularly his father, Reggie, and his brother Keith. He recalled with humor that, despite decades in cricket, his memorable “Man of the Match” performance involved hitting two sixes and two fours with a handmade bat during a backyard game in Guyana. The anecdote captures an important distinction in his career.  
  
Aaron’s impact on cricket did not come principally through runs scored or wickets taken.  
  
It came through service.  
  
**Recognition by the New York Cricket Community**  
That service was recognized again in July 2025, when Aaron was among three New York cricket administrators honored with the Recognizing Excellence in NY Cricket Award.  
  
The recognition highlighted his extensive administrative record and his ability to work with people with differing viewpoints to achieve shared goals.  
  
The honor acknowledged his contributions to cricket development, community engagement, and the growth of women’s cricket.  
  
By then, his résumé encompassed club, league, regional, and national administration; international team management; championship-winning women’s cricket; journalism; community service; and decades of advocacy for the sport.  
  
**Continuing the Mission Through AWCSG**  
Aaron’s commitment to women’s cricket continued beyond his national-team management assignments.  
  
Earlier this year, he became actively involved as a director and organizing committee member of the American Women’s Cricket Support Group (AWCSG), a nonprofit organization established to support the holistic development of women and girls in cricket in the United States.  
  
AWCSG’s mission extends beyond simply providing match platforms. Its programming emphasizes competitive opportunities, education, leadership, mental agility, team-building, and physical development.  
  
AWCSG held its inaugural Premier Women’s T20 tournament in Florida in April this year, and the ICC sanctioned it. The highly successful tournament provided another platform for female cricketers to compete, develop, and demonstrate their abilities.   
  
John Aaron managed the tournament’s unbeaten champions, the Freedom Flyers, and secured the title sponsorship for the inaugural T20 tournament. The AWCSG has scheduled its second edition for October 9–12, 2026, in Groveland, FL.  
  
For Aaron, the initiative continues principles evident throughout his cricket career: creating opportunities, strengthening pathways, and helping female athletes develop both on and off the cricket field.  
  
**More Than Just Cricket**  
Perhaps the most appropriate way to understand John Aaron’s contribution to American cricket is through the philosophy he has long embraced at Atlantis: Atlantis…more than just cricket!  
  
**His career demonstrates what those words can mean.  
  
Cricket can provide competition, but it can also create friendships and communities.  
  
It can develop athletes, but it can also develop leaders.**  
  
A cricket club can win championships, but it can also award scholarships, assist families, introduce children to a new sport, and create pathways toward national representation.  
  
And a national team can pursue victories while also giving young women opportunities previous generations never had.  
  
The numbers provide one measure of Aaron’s cricket journey: five GWCA Women’s T20 championships in seven attempts; eight USA national representatives from Atlantis women’s teams; three successful ICC Americas campaigns; a 3–2 USA Under-19 series victory in the UAE; a victory over ICC Full Member Zimbabwe in Florida; successful competition against six Caribbean representative teams; two bilateral series victories over West Indies Under-19 squads; participation as Team Manager at the inaugural ICC Under-19 Women’s T20 World Cup; service at club, league, regional, and national levels; and recognition as a Cricket Hall of Fame inductee.  
  
Yet numbers and titles tell only part of the story.  
  
From Atlantis Cricket Club–NY to international cricket grounds across the Americas, the Caribbean, the Middle East, Africa, and Europe, Aaron’s journey has included governance, journalism, community service, championship-winning team management, and developing generations of cricketers.  
  
More than four decades after becoming involved in American cricket administration, he still regards the work not principally in terms of positions held, championships won, or honors received, but as service to the game.  
  
It is therefore fitting that one description has followed him through the years: **A Servant of Cricket.**  
  
And perhaps that remains the simplest description of John Aaron’s cricket career—a lifetime devoted to helping ensure that the game, and the people who play it, are left stronger for the generations that follow.
